sections.md:
Money is something that can act as a medium of exchange in transactions. Before coins came into use, a variety of objects were used as money: Indians used **grains and cattle**. Thereafter came **metallic coins** — gold, silver, copper — a phase which continued well into the last century.

### Currency
Modern forms of money include **currency — paper notes and coins**. Unlike the things used as money earlier, modern currency is **not made of precious metal** such as gold, silver and copper, and unlike grain and cattle it is neither of everyday use. The modern currency is without any use of its own. Then why is it accepted as a medium of exchange?

It is accepted because it is **authorised by the government** of the country. In India, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** issues currency notes on behalf of the central government. As per Indian law, **no other individual or organisation is allowed to issue currency**. Moreover, the law **legalises the use of rupees** as a medium of payment that **cannot be refused** in settling transactions in India. No individual in India can legally refuse a payment made in rupees. Hence the rupee is widely accepted as a medium of exchange.

### Deposits with banks
The other form in which people hold money is as **deposits with banks**. At a point of time, people need only some currency for their day-to-day needs. For instance, workers who receive their salaries at the end of each month have extra cash at the beginning of the month. What do people do with this extra cash? They deposit it with the banks by opening a bank account in their name. Banks accept the deposits and also **pay an amount as interest** on the deposits. In this way people's money is safe with the banks and it earns interest. People also have the provision to **withdraw the money as and when they require**. Since the deposits in the bank accounts can be withdrawn **on demand**, these deposits are called **demand deposits**.

### Cheques and digital payments
Demand deposits offer another interesting facility, which lends them the essential characteristics of money. You would have heard of payments being made by **cheques** instead of cash. For payment through cheque, the payer who has an account with the bank makes out a cheque for a specific amount. **A cheque is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the person's account to the person in whose name the cheque has been issued.**

Thus we see that demand deposits share the essential features of money. The facility of cheques against demand deposits makes it possible to directly settle payments without the use of cash. Since demand deposits are accepted widely as a means of payment, along with currency, they constitute **money in the modern economy**. But remember the role of banks: if not for the banks, there would be no demand deposits and no payments by cheques.

Today the same idea powers **UPI, debit cards, NEFT and RTGS** — they all move demand deposits from one account to another. (Box idea: in a cheque payment, a shoe manufacturer M pays leather supplier S ₹20,000 by cheque; S deposits it in his bank; the money is transferred from M's account to S's account; M's balance falls by ₹20,000 and S's rises by ₹20,000.)

check.q: Why is the rupee note accepted as money even though the paper has little value?
options: It is authorised by the government and by law cannot be refused in India
check.why: The RBI issues currency on behalf of the government and the law makes the rupee a payment that no one in India can refuse.

sections.md:
What do banks do with the deposits they accept from the public? There is an interesting mechanism at work here.

Banks keep only a **small proportion of their deposits as cash** with themselves. For example, banks in India these days hold about **15% of their deposits as cash** (as per the textbook). This is kept as provision to pay the depositors who might come to withdraw money from the bank on any given day. Since on any particular day, only some of its many depositors come to withdraw cash, the bank is able to manage with this cash.

Banks use the **major portion of the deposits to extend loans**. There is a huge demand for loans for various economic activities. Banks make use of the deposits to meet the loan requirements of the people. In this way, **banks mediate between those who have surplus funds (the depositors) and those who are in need of these funds (the borrowers)**.

Banks charge a **higher interest rate on loans than what they offer on deposits**. The **difference between what is charged from borrowers and what is paid to depositors is their main source of income**.

### Worked idea
Suppose a bank pays 6% a year on deposits and charges 10% on loans. A depositor puts in ₹1,00,000; the bank keeps ₹15,000 as cash and lends ₹85,000.
- Interest paid to depositor in a year: 6% of 1,00,000 = ₹6,000.
- Interest earned from borrower: 10% of 85,000 = ₹8,500.
- Bank's margin: 8,500 − 6,000 = ₹2,500 (before its own costs).

sections.md:
A large number of transactions in our day-to-day activities involve **credit** in some form or the other. **Credit (loan)** refers to an agreement in which the **lender supplies the borrower with money, goods or services in return for the promise of future payment**.

The textbook tells two short stories (retold here in our own words).

### (1) Festival season — Salim the shoe manufacturer
It is festival season, two months away. **Salim**, a shoe manufacturer in Agra, has received an order from a trader in the city for 3,000 pairs of shoes to be delivered in a month's time. To complete production on time, he has to hire a few more workers for stitching and pasting work. He has to purchase raw materials. To meet these expenses, Salim obtains **supplies of leather on credit** from the leather supplier (promising to pay later) and also takes a **cash advance** from the large trader as payment in advance for one-third of the order, with a promise to deliver the whole order later.

By the end of the month, Salim delivers the order, makes a good profit, and **repays the money** he had borrowed. Credit here helped him **meet the ongoing expenses of production, complete production on time, and increase his earnings**. **Credit plays a vital and positive role** in this situation.

### (2) Swapna's problem — the debt trap
**Swapna**, a small farmer, grows groundnut on her three acres of land. She takes a loan from a **moneylender** to meet the expenses of cultivation, hoping that her harvest would help repay the loan. Midway through the season, the crop is hit by **pests** and the crop fails. Though Swapna sprays her fields with expensive pesticides, it makes little difference. She is unable to repay the moneylender, and the debt grows large over the year into a big amount. Next year, Swapna takes a fresh loan for cultivation. It is a normal crop that year, but the earnings are not enough to cover the old loan. She is caught in debt. She has to **sell a part of her land** to pay off the debt. Thereafter she stops taking loans and works as an agricultural labourer.

Unlike Salim, for Swapna the failure of the crop made loan repayment impossible. She had to sell part of the land. **Credit, instead of helping Swapna improve her earnings, left her worse off.** This is an example of what is commonly called **debt-trap**.

**Lesson:** In one situation credit helps to increase earnings and the person is better off than before. In another situation, because of the **crop failure**, credit pushes the person into a debt trap. Whether credit would be useful or not depends on the **risks in the situation** and whether there is some **support, in case of loss**.

left.title: Salim (Agra, shoes)
points: Credit: leather on credit + advance from trader
Used to buy inputs and hire workers
Order delivered on time, good profit

right.title: Swapna (groundnut farmer)
points: Could not repay; debt grew; fresh loan
Sold land; worse off — debt trap

check.q: Why did credit push Swapna into a debt trap?
options: She spent the loan on a festival
Crop failure made repayment impossible and there was no support for the loss
check.why: Her crop was destroyed by pests, so she lacked income to repay; with high-interest moneylender debt and no insurance, the debt kept growing.

sections.md:
Every loan agreement specifies an **interest rate** which the borrower must pay to the lender along with the repayment of the principal. In addition, lenders may demand **collateral** (security) against loans.

**Collateral** is an asset that the borrower owns (such as land, building, vehicle, livestock, deposits with banks) and uses this as a **guarantee to a lender until the loan is repaid**. If the borrower fails to repay the loan, the lender has the **right to sell the asset or collateral** to obtain payment. Property such as land titles, deposits with banks, livestock are some common examples of collateral used for borrowing.

**Interest rate, collateral and documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment together comprise what is called the terms of credit.** The terms of credit vary substantially from one credit arrangement to another. They may vary depending on the nature of the lender and the borrower.

### A textbook example — Megha's home loan
In the textbook's example, **Megha** takes a loan of ₹5 lakh from a bank to purchase a house. The annual interest rate on the loan is 12% and the loan is to be repaid in 10 years in monthly instalments. Megha had to submit to the bank documents showing her employment records and salary before the bank agreed to give her the loan. The bank retained as collateral the papers of the new house, which will be returned to Megha only when she repays the entire loan with interest. So the terms of her credit are: **interest rate 12%; collateral — house papers; documentation — employment and salary records; mode of repayment — monthly instalments over 10 years.**

**Simple interest check (for understanding only):** on ₹5,00,000 at 12% a year, one year's interest = ₹60,000. (Actual home-loan EMIs use reducing-balance calculations, so total interest over 10 years is not simply 10 × ₹60,000.)

check.q: Which of these is NOT one of the terms of credit?
options: The colour of the cheque book
check.why: Terms of credit consist of the interest rate, collateral, documentation requirements and mode of repayment.

sections.h: Variety of credit arrangements — the village of Sonpur
sections.md:
The textbook takes us to a village, **Sonpur**, to see different sources of credit. (Retold in our own words.)

### Shyamal — a small farmer
**Shyamal** cultivates a small plot of land (about 1.5 acres). Every season he needs loans to meet expenses of cultivation. Earlier, he used to borrow from a village **moneylender** who charges an interest rate of **5% per month (60% per year)**. For the past few years Shyamal has been borrowing from an **agricultural trader** in the village at a lower rate. The trader supplies agricultural inputs on credit and in return demands that the farmers **sell their crop to him** when it is harvested. The trader can then purchase the crop at a **low price**, and later sell it at a higher price, earning a profit. Shyamal gets a loan at the start of the season but has to sell his crop at the price the trader sets.

### Arun — a larger landowner
**Arun** has 7 acres of land. He is among the few people in Sonpur to receive **bank credit** for cultivation. The interest rate on the loan is **8.5% per annum** and can be repaid anytime in the next three years. Arun plans to repay the loan after harvest by selling a part of the crop. He then intends to store the rest of the potatoes in a cold storage and apply for a fresh loan from the bank against the cold storage receipt. The bank offers this facility to farmers who have taken credit from it.

### Rama — a landless labourer
**Rama** works as an agricultural labourer. There are several months in the year when she has no work and needs credit to meet daily expenses. Expenses on sudden illnesses or functions in the family are also met through loans. She has to depend on her **employer, a medium landowner** in Sonpur, for credit, who charges an interest rate of **5% per month**. Rama repays the loan by working for the landowner. Over the years she has borrowed again and again, and her total debt keeps rising. The landowner treats her badly, and she continues to work for him because she has no other options.

**Observation:** the people of Sonpur who are poor depend on **informal sources** — moneylenders, traders, employers — at high interest rates, with conditions that can trap them. Only the better-off, like Arun, get **cheap bank credit**.

Compare one year's interest on ₹10,000:
| Source | Rate | Interest in one year |
|---|---|---|
| Moneylender / employer | 5% per month = 60% per year | ₹6,000 |
| Bank | 8.5% per year | ₹850 |

The poor pay **about seven times** as much interest on the same amount (6,000 ÷ 850 ≈ 7.1).

sections.md:
The various types of loans can be conveniently grouped as **formal sector loans** and **informal sector loans**.
- **Formal:** loans from **banks and cooperatives**.
- **Informal:** **moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends** etc.

### Supervision
The **Reserve Bank of India supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans**. For instance, banks have to maintain a minimum cash balance out of the deposits they receive. The RBI monitors that the banks actually maintain the cash balance. Similarly, the RBI sees that the banks give loans **not just to profit-making businesses and traders but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries, small borrowers** etc. Periodically, banks have to submit information to the RBI on how much they are lending, to whom, at what interest rate, etc.

There is **no organisation which supervises the credit activities of lenders in the informal sector**. They can lend at whatever interest rate they choose. There is no one to stop them from using unfair means to get their money back.

### Why informal credit is costly
Compared to the formal lenders, most of the informal lenders charge a **much higher interest on loans**. Thus the cost to the borrower of informal loans is much higher. **Higher cost of borrowing means a larger part of the earnings of the borrowers is used to repay the loan.** Hence, borrowers have less income left for themselves. In certain cases, the high interest rate for borrowing can mean that the amount to be repaid is greater than the income of the borrower. This could lead to **increasing debt and debt trap**. Also, people who might wish to start an enterprise by borrowing may not do so because of the high cost of borrowing.

For these reasons, **banks and cooperative societies need to lend more**. This would lead to higher incomes, and many people could then borrow cheaply for a variety of needs. They could grow crops, do business, set up small-scale industries etc. They could set up new industries or trade in goods. **Cheap and affordable credit is crucial for the country's development.**

### Who gets formal credit?
The textbook's graph (based on survey data) shows that **rich households get most of their credit from formal sources**, while **poor households depend largely on informal sources** — the poorest households in urban areas get only a small fraction of their loans from formal sources, compared with the richest who get the great majority from formal sources.

Why? Banks are not present everywhere in rural India. Even when they are present, getting a loan from a bank is much more difficult than taking a loan from informal sources: bank loans require proper **documents and collateral**. **Absence of collateral** is one of the major reasons which prevents the poor from getting bank loans. Informal lenders such as moneylenders, on the other hand, know the borrowers personally and hence are often willing to give a loan without collateral. The borrowers can, if necessary, approach the moneylenders even without repaying their earlier loans. However, the moneylenders charge very high rates of interest, keep no records of the transactions and harass the poor borrowers.

**Conclusion:** formal credit needs to expand, and it must be **distributed more equally** so that the poor can benefit from the cheaper loans. It is necessary that **both formal sector loans increase and that everyone receives these loans**.

right.title: Informal (moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives)
points: High interest; may use unfair means

check.q: Who supervises formal sources of credit in India?
check.why: The RBI monitors banks' cash balances and lending, including loans to small borrowers; informal lenders are unsupervised.

sections.md:
In the previous section we saw that poor households are still dependent on informal sources of credit. Why? Banks are not present everywhere; getting a bank loan is difficult because of collateral and documents. Moneylenders charge very high rates and keep no records.

In recent years, people have tried out some newer ways of providing loans to the poor. The idea is to **organise rural poor, in particular women, into small Self-Help Groups (SHGs)** and **pool (collect) their savings**.

### How an SHG works
- A typical SHG has **15–20 members**, usually belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly.
- Saving per member varies from **₹25 to ₹100 or more**, depending on the ability of the people to save.
- Members can take **small loans from the group itself** to meet their needs. The group charges interest on these loans, but this is **still less than what the moneylender charges**.
- After a year or two, if the group is regular in savings, it becomes **eligible for availing loans from the bank**. Loan is sanctioned **in the name of the group** and is meant to create **self-employment opportunities** for the members. For instance, small loans are provided to the members for releasing mortgaged land, for meeting working capital needs (buying seeds, fertilisers, raw materials like bamboo and cloth), for housing materials, for acquiring assets like sewing machines, handlooms, cattle etc.
- Most of the important decisions regarding the savings and loan activities are **taken by the group members**. The group decides as regards the loans to be granted — the purpose, amount, interest to be charged, repayment schedule etc. Also, it is the group which is **responsible for the repayment** of the loan. Any case of non-repayment of loan by any one member is followed up seriously by other members in the group. Because of this feature, **banks are willing to lend to the poor women** when organised in SHGs, even though they have no collateral as such.

### Benefits
Thus SHGs help borrowers **overcome the problem of lack of collateral**. They can get timely loans for a variety of purposes and at a reasonable interest rate. Moreover, SHGs are the **building blocks of organisation of the rural poor**. Not only does it help women to become **financially self-reliant**, the regular meetings of the group provide a platform to discuss and act on a variety of social issues such as **health, nutrition, domestic violence** etc.

### The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh
The textbook's box describes the **Grameen Bank of Bangladesh**, started in the **1970s** as a small project. By 2006 it had over 6 million borrowers in about 40,000 villages spread across Bangladesh, and **almost all of the borrowers are women** who belong to the poorest sections of the society. These borrowers have proved that not only are poor women reliable borrowers, they can start and run a variety of small income-generating activities. The founder of the Grameen Bank, **Professor Muhammad Yunus**, was the recipient of the **2006 Nobel Peace Prize**. The idea he put forward: credit should be made available to everyone — *that the poor can be trusted with loans*.

workedExamples.q: Rama borrows ₹5,000 from her employer at 5% per month. Ignoring compounding, how much interest does she owe after one year? Compare with a bank at 9% per year.
A bank receives deposits of ₹10 crore and keeps 15% as cash. How much can it lend?
An SHG of 20 women each saves ₹50 a month. What is the group's pooled saving after one year?
workedExamples.answer: ₹12,000 (before any interest earned on internal loans)

summary: Money is a medium of exchange; it removes the need for the double coincidence of wants in barter.
Earlier forms: grain, cattle, metal coins; modern forms: currency and demand deposits.
Currency is accepted because it is authorised by the government; the RBI issues notes; the rupee cannot legally be refused in India.
Demand deposits can be withdrawn on demand and used via cheques (and today digital payments), so they are money.
Banks keep about 15% of deposits as cash and lend the rest; the interest-rate gap is their main income.
Credit is an agreement to supply money, goods or services in return for future payment.
Salim's case shows credit raising earnings; Swapna's shows a debt trap after crop failure.
Terms of credit: interest rate, collateral, documentation, mode of repayment.
In Sonpur, the poor depend on moneylenders, traders and employers at high rates; the better-off get bank loans.
Formal credit (banks, cooperatives) is supervised by the RBI; informal credit is unsupervised and costly.
Rich households get most loans from formal sources; poor households rely on informal sources, mainly due to lack of collateral.
Cheap and affordable credit, more equally distributed, is crucial for development.
Self-Help Groups of 15–20 members pool savings, lend internally, and borrow from banks without collateral.
SHGs empower women socially and financially; the Grameen Bank (Muhammad Yunus, Nobel Peace Prize 2006) is a famous model.

rd-school-c10-social-c.e4-globalisation.title: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
rd-school-c10-social-c.e4-globalisation.subtitle: Your phone was designed in one country, assembled in another and sold in a third — here's how the world got so connected

sections.md:
Until the middle of the twentieth century, production was largely organised **within countries**. What crossed borders were raw materials, food and finished products. Colonies such as India exported raw cotton, indigo and jute and imported finished cloth and machines from Britain. Trade was the main link between distant countries.

The new player is the **Multinational Corporation (MNC)**: a company that **owns or controls production in more than one nation**. MNCs set up offices and factories for production in regions where they can get **cheap labour and other resources**. This is done so that the cost of production is low and the MNC can earn greater profits.

Consider a large MNC producing industrial equipment. It designs its products in research centres in the **United States**, has the components manufactured in **China**, ships them to **Mexico and Eastern Europe** where the products are assembled, and sells the finished products all over the world. Its customer care is carried out through **call centres located in India**. Each part of the work is done where it is cheapest or most efficient.

**Why do MNCs choose a particular location?** They look for:

1. **Closeness to markets** — being near the buyers.
2. **Skilled and unskilled labour at low cost.**
3. **Assured availability of other factors of production** — power, water, transport, raw materials.
4. **Government policies that look after their interests** — low taxes, easy rules.

China, for example, offered cheap labour and huge factories; India offered a large English-speaking, educated workforce for services; Mexico is next door to the giant US market.

**Investment** means money spent on buying assets such as land, building, machines and other equipment. Investment made by MNCs is called **foreign investment**. Any investment is made with the hope that these assets will earn profits.

check.q: An MNC is a company that…
options: Sells only in its home country
Owns or controls production in more than one nation
check.why: Multinationals spread production across several countries to cut costs and reach markets.

sections.md:
MNCs do not always build their own factories from scratch. They spread production and interact with local producers in several ways:

1. **Joint production with local companies.** The MNC sets up production jointly with some of the local companies. The benefit to the local company is twofold: the MNC can provide **money for additional investment** (like buying new machines for faster production), and it brings with it the **latest technology** for production.
2. **Buying up local companies** and then expanding production. MNCs with huge wealth can do this easily. Example: **Cargill Foods**, a very large American MNC, bought over smaller Indian companies such as **Parakh Foods**. Parakh Foods had built a large marketing network in various parts of India, and its brand was well-respected. It had four oil refineries, whose control shifted to Cargill. Cargill is now one of the largest producers of edible oil in India, making millions of pouches daily.
3. **Placing orders with small producers.** Large MNCs in developed countries place orders for production with small producers. **Garments, footwear and sports items** are industries where production is carried out by a large number of small producers around the world. The products are supplied to the MNCs, which then sell these under their own **brand names** to customers. These large MNCs have tremendous power to determine **price, quality, delivery and labour conditions** for these distant producers.

So, by setting up partnerships with local companies, by using local companies for supplies, and by closely competing with or buying up local companies, MNCs are **exerting a strong influence on production at these distant locations**. Production in these widely dispersed locations is getting **interlinked**.

**Did you know?** Some of the largest MNCs have annual revenues larger than the entire government budgets of many developing countries. Size gives them bargaining power with governments and suppliers alike.

check.q: Cargill Foods buying Parakh Foods is an example of MNCs…
check.why: Cargill acquired an existing Indian firm with a strong brand and network, then expanded production.

sections.h: Case study: Ford Motors in India
sections.md:
The textbook uses the American automobile giant **Ford Motors** to show how an MNC thinks.

- Ford is one of the world's largest automobile manufacturers, with production spread over many countries.
- It came to India in **1995** and spent about **₹1700 crore** to set up a large plant near **Chennai**, in collaboration with **Mahindra and Mahindra**, a major Indian manufacturer of jeeps and trucks.
- By the early 2000s Ford was selling tens of thousands of cars in Indian markets, and also exporting cars and car parts from India to countries such as South Africa, Mexico and Brazil.
- The company wanted to develop Ford India as a **component supplying base** for its other plants across the globe.

Why did Ford choose India? A growing market of car buyers; skilled engineers and workers available at lower wages than in the USA; a good port at Chennai for exports; and an Indian partner who knew the local market.

Is Ford an MNC? Yes — it owns or controls production in more than one country. Using India as a base for components for plants elsewhere shows how production is **interlinked** across borders: a car in Brazil may contain parts made in Tamil Nadu.

*(Note: business decisions change over time — in 2021 Ford announced it would stop making cars in India. Globalisation also means firms can leave as quickly as they come, which is a lesson in itself.)*

check.q: Ford using its Chennai plant to supply parts to plants in other countries shows…
check.why: Parts made in one country feed assembly in others, linking production globally.

sections.h: Foreign trade and integration of markets
sections.md:
For a long time, **foreign trade** has been the main channel connecting countries. In history you read about trade routes connecting India and South Asia to markets both in the East and West — the Silk Route, the spice trade of Kerala's ports — and the extensive trade that took place along them. It was trading interests that attracted various trading companies such as the **East India Company** to India.

What is the basic function of foreign trade? Foreign trade creates an **opportunity for producers to reach beyond the markets of their own countries**. Producers can sell their produce not only in markets located within the country but can also compete in markets located in other countries. Similarly, for buyers, import of goods produced in another country is one way of **expanding the choice of goods** beyond those domestically produced.

**Example: Chinese toys in India.** Chinese manufacturers learn of an opportunity to export toys to India, where toys are sold at a high price. They start exporting plastic toys. Buyers in India now have the option of choosing between Indian and Chinese toys. Because of cheaper prices and new designs, Chinese toys become popular. Within a year, a large share of toy shops replace Indian toys with Chinese ones.

- **Indian buyers** gain: more choice, lower prices.
- **Chinese toy makers** gain: a bigger market and more business.
- **Indian toy makers** lose: they face competition, and many find their toys are not selling.

With the opening of trade, goods travel from one market to another. Choice of goods in the markets rises. **Prices of similar goods in the two markets tend to become equal.** And producers in the two countries now **closely compete** against each other even though they are separated by thousands of kilometres. Foreign trade thus results in **connecting the markets**, or **integration of markets**, in different countries.

sections.md:
In the past few decades, more and more MNCs have been looking for locations around the world that would be cheap for their production. **Foreign investment by MNCs in these countries has been rising.** At the same time, **foreign trade between countries has been rising rapidly**. A large part of foreign trade is also controlled by MNCs — for example, the car manufacturing plant of Ford in India not only produces cars for the Indian market but also exports cars and parts.

The result of greater foreign investment and greater foreign trade has been **greater integration of production and markets across countries**. Globalisation is this process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries. MNCs are playing a **major role** in it.

More and more goods and services, investments and technology are moving between countries. Most regions of the world are in closer contact with each other than a few decades back.

Besides goods, services, investments and technology, there is one more way countries can be connected: **movement of people** between countries. People usually move from one country to another in search of better income, better jobs or better education. In the past few decades, however, there has **not been much increase** in the movement of people between countries due to various restrictions — visas, work permits, immigration rules.

| Channel | Example |
|---|---|
| Goods | Chinese toys sold in Indian shops |
| Services | An Indian call centre answering US customers |
| Investment | Ford's ₹1700 crore plant near Chennai |
| Technology | A Korean firm bringing new phone-making machines to Noida |
| People | An Indian nurse working in the Gulf (restricted by rules) |

check.q: Which channel of globalisation has grown the LEAST in recent decades?
check.why: Visa and immigration restrictions have kept the movement of people far more limited than flows of goods and capital.

sections.md:
**Factor 1: Technology.** Rapid improvement in technology has been one major factor that has stimulated globalisation.

- **Transport technology.** The past fifty years have seen several improvements, making much faster delivery of goods across long distances possible at lower costs. **Containers** — big standard boxes loaded on ships, rail and trucks — have led to huge reductions in port handling costs and increased the speed with which exports reach markets. Air transport has become cheaper too.
- **Information and communication technology (IT).** Telecommunication facilities (telegraph, telephone including mobile phones, fax) are used to contact one another around the world, to access information instantly and to communicate from remote areas — made possible by **satellite communication devices**. Computers and the **internet** let you obtain and share information on almost anything, send instant e-mail and talk (voice-mail) across the world at negligible costs.

**Box: Using IT in globalisation.** A news magazine published for London readers is to be designed and printed in Delhi. The text is sent through the internet to the Delhi office. Designers in Delhi get orders on how to design the magazine from the office in London using telecommunication facilities. Designing is done on a computer; after printing, the magazines are sent by air to London. Even the payment of money for designing and printing from a bank in London to a bank in Delhi is done instantly through the internet (e-banking)! Both **production of services** and their delivery now happen across borders.

**Factor 2: Liberalisation of foreign trade and foreign investment policy.** Suppose the Indian government puts a tax on import of toys. Buyers would have to pay this tax, so Chinese toys become costlier and imports fall; Indian toy makers would prosper. Tax on imports is one example of a **trade barrier**. It is called a barrier because some restriction has been set up. Governments use trade barriers to **increase or decrease (regulate) foreign trade** and to decide what kinds of goods, and how much of each, should come into the country.

After Independence, the Government of India put barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment. This was considered necessary to **protect the producers within the country from foreign competition**. Industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s, and competition from imports at that stage would not have allowed them to come up. India allowed imports of only essential items such as machinery, fertilisers and petroleum.

Starting around **1991**, some far-reaching changes in policy were made. The government decided that the time had come for Indian producers to **compete with producers around the globe**. It felt competition would improve the performance of producers, who would have to improve their quality. This decision was supported by powerful international organisations. Barriers on foreign trade and investment were removed to a large extent: goods could be imported and exported easily, and foreign companies could set up factories and offices here.

Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is what is known as **liberalisation**. With liberalisation, businesses are allowed to make decisions freely about what they wish to import or export. The government imposes much fewer restrictions than before and is therefore said to be more liberal.

items.what: India protects young industries with trade barriers
First container ship voyage (USA) — transport revolution begins
New Economic Policy: liberalisation of trade and investment
WTO set up; India a founder member; internet arrives in India
Rapid growth of IT services and outsourcing in India
Special Economic Zones Act

fig.caption: India's journey into the global economy

keyTerms: Globalisation — integration of production and markets across countries
Trade barrier — government restriction such as an import tax
Liberalisation — removing government barriers to trade and investment
Container — standard box that cut port handling costs

check.q: Why did India impose trade barriers after Independence?
options: To protect young domestic industries from foreign competition
check.why: New industries of the 1950s–60s would not have survived open competition from established foreign producers.

sections.md:
We have seen that the liberalisation of foreign trade and investment in India was supported by some very powerful international organisations. These organisations say all barriers to foreign trade and investment are harmful and there should be no barriers. Trade between countries should be 'free'.

The **World Trade Organisation (WTO)**, set up in **1995**, is one such organisation whose aim is to **liberalise international trade**. At the initiative of developed countries, the WTO **establishes rules regarding international trade** and sees that these rules are obeyed. About **164 countries** of the world are currently members (the textbook says 'about 160').

Though the WTO is supposed to allow free trade for all, in practice it is seen that **developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers**. On the other hand, WTO rules have **forced developing countries to remove trade barriers**.

**Box: Debate on farm subsidies.** Agriculture provides jobs to a large share of India's workers. Compare this with the USA, where farming's share in production and employment is tiny — yet the US government gives massive sums every year to its farmers as **subsidies**, and other developed countries do the same. With this money, US farmers can sell farm products at **abnormally low prices**. These surplus products are sold in other countries at low prices, adversely affecting farmers there. Developing countries are asking: *we have reduced trade barriers under WTO rules; why are developed countries still protecting their farmers?*

So developing countries argue that the WTO should work for **fair rules**, not just 'free' trade that suits the rich.

check.q: The main complaint of developing countries about the WTO is that…
options: Developed countries keep subsidies and barriers while poor countries must remove theirs
check.why: Rules are applied unequally: rich nations still subsidise farmers heavily while pushing poor nations to open up.

sections.md:
Globalisation and greater competition among producers — both local and foreign — has been of advantage to **consumers**, particularly the **well-off sections in urban areas**. There is greater choice before them, and they enjoy improved quality and lower prices for several products. These people enjoy much higher standards of living than before.

**MNCs** have increased their investments in India over the past 20 years, which means investing in India has been beneficial for them. MNCs have been interested in industries such as **cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food** and services such as **banking** in urban areas. These products have a large number of well-off buyers. In these industries and services, **new jobs** have been created. Local companies supplying raw materials to these industries have also prospered.

**Top Indian companies** have been able to benefit from the increased competition. They have invested in newer technology and production methods and raised their production standards. Some have gained from successful collaborations with foreign companies.

Moreover, globalisation has enabled some large Indian companies to **emerge as multinationals themselves** — **Tata Motors** (automobiles), **Infosys** (IT), **Ranbaxy** (medicines), **Asian Paints** (paints), **Sundaram Fasteners** (nuts and bolts) are spreading operations worldwide.

Globalisation has also created new opportunities for companies providing **services**, particularly those involving IT. The Indian company producing a magazine for a London company, and call centres, are some examples. A host of services such as **data entry, accounting, administrative tasks and engineering** are now being done cheaply in countries such as India and exported to developed countries.

**Steps to attract foreign investment.** In recent years, the central and state governments are taking special steps. Industrial zones called **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** are being set up, with world-class facilities: electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreational and educational facilities. Companies who set up production units in SEZs **do not have to pay taxes for an initial period of five years**. The government has also allowed **flexibility in labour laws** — instead of hiring workers on a regular basis, companies hire workers 'flexibly' for short periods when there is intense pressure of work, to reduce labour cost.

left.title: Gains
points: More choice, better quality, lower prices for consumers
Indian firms became MNCs (Tata Motors, Infosys)

right.title: Costs
points: Units closed: toys, batteries, dairy, oil
Long hours, low wages in export units

check.q: Companies in an SEZ get which special benefit?
options: No taxes for an initial period of five years
check.why: Tax holidays and world-class infrastructure are offered to attract investment into SEZs.

sections.h: The other side: small producers and workers
sections.md:
Yet the benefits of globalisation have **not been shared equally**. For a large number of **small producers and workers**, rising competition has meant hardship.

**Box: Ravi's small industry (retold).** Ravi took a bank loan in 1992 to start a small company making **capacitors** — electronic parts used in TVs and other appliances — in Hosur, Tamil Nadu. In three years he expanded and employed about twenty workers. His capacitors were bought by large Indian TV companies. But in 2001 the government removed restrictions on imports of capacitors as part of its WTO commitments. His main buyers, the TV companies, began buying cheaper imported capacitors, and some TV makers themselves shut or were bought by MNCs that imported parts. Ravi's sales dropped to less than half. He had to cut his workforce to just seven workers.

The textbook notes that many small units were hit hard: **batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil**. Several units shut down, rendering many workers jobless. Small industries employ the largest number of workers in India after agriculture, so this matters.

**Box: Sushila's story — flexible labour (retold).** Sushila worked for many years in a large **garment export** factory in Delhi as a permanent worker. She was paid enough to manage, had **provident fund, medical insurance and overtime pay**. But over time her factory shut; she found work in another unit — this time a **temporary** job. Now she works up to **ten hours a day**, sometimes at night, with no extra pay, no job security, and wages that are lower than before.

Why? Large MNCs in the garment industry in Europe and America order products from Indian exporters. These MNCs, with worldwide networks, look for the **cheapest goods** to maximise profits. To get these large orders, Indian garment exporters try hard to **cut their own costs**. Since cost of raw materials cannot be reduced, exporters try to **cut labour costs**. Where earlier a factory used to employ workers on a permanent basis, now they employ workers only on a **temporary** basis so that they do not have to pay workers for the whole year. Workers also have to put in long working hours and work night shifts on a regular basis during the peak season.

While competition among exporters helped MNCs make large profits, workers were **denied their fair share** of benefits. Most employment generated in recent years is in the **unorganised sector**, and even the organised sector increasingly has unorganised-type conditions.

check.q: Why do garment exporters hire workers 'flexibly'?
options: To cut labour costs so they can win orders from MNCs at low prices
Because the law forbids permanent jobs
check.why: Under price pressure from MNC buyers, exporters cut the one cost they control — labour — by making jobs temporary.

sections.md:
The evidence suggests that globalisation is **not good for everyone** in its present form. People with education, skill and wealth have made the best use of the new opportunities. On the other hand, there are many people who have not shared the benefits.

Since globalisation is now a reality, the question is how to make it more **fair**. **Fair globalisation** would create opportunities for all, and also ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared better.

**Role of government:**

- Its policies must protect the interests not only of the rich and powerful but **all the people** in the country.
- It can ensure that **labour laws are properly implemented** and workers get their rights.
- It can **support small producers** to improve their performance till the time they become strong enough to compete.
- If necessary, it can use **trade and investment barriers**.
- It can **negotiate at the WTO for 'fairer rules'**.
- It can **align with other developing countries** with similar interests to fight against the domination of developed countries in the WTO.

**Role of people:** In the past few years, **massive campaigns and representation by people's organisations** have influenced important decisions relating to trade and investment at the WTO. This has demonstrated that people can also play an important role in the struggle for fair globalisation.

> The question is not whether to globalise, but how to make globalisation work for the many and not only for the few.

**Think it through (textbook-style activity):** Make a two-column chart of people you know — a shopkeeper, a software engineer, a farmer, a factory worker, a student. For each, note one way globalisation helped them and one way it hurt them. You will discover that the same process looks very different from different chairs.

check.q: Which is a step towards fair globalisation?
options: Supporting small producers and enforcing labour rights
check.why: Fair globalisation shares benefits by protecting workers and helping small producers compete.

parts.md: In 1990, Harpreet's grandfather ran a small workshop in Ludhiana making bicycle bells and woollen mittens. At Diwali the family bought one new thing — usually a steel almirah or a radio — after waiting months. The shops in Chaura Bazaar sold Indian-made goods, few brands, high prices. Imports were rare and costly because of heavy import duties. His workshop was safe: no foreign rival could reach his customers.

In 2024, Harpreet's Diwali shopping list is ordered on a phone. The phone is a Korean brand assembled in Noida; its chips come from Taiwan; its software from California. The lights are Chinese, cheap and bright. Harpreet's elder sister answers calls for an American bank from a Mohali office. His uncle, though, closed the bell workshop in 2006 — imported parts were cheaper. Same family, same city: one member gained a well-paid service job, another lost a business. That, in one household, is globalisation — and the reason the chapter ends by asking for it to be fair.

workedExamples.q: A Chinese toy costs ₹400 to import. India puts a 25% import tax on it. What is the price after tax? If the tax is removed, how much cheaper is it?
workedExamples.answer: ₹500 with tax; ₹100 cheaper when the barrier is removed

workedExamples.q: An MNC can make a shirt in Country X for ₹300 (labour ₹120) or Country Y for ₹240 (labour ₹60). Other costs are equal. Where will it produce and why?
workedExamples.answer: Country Y, because cheaper labour saves ₹60 per shirt.

workedExamples.q: Ravi employed 20 workers; after imports were opened he kept 7. What percentage of jobs were lost?

summary: Globalisation is the rapid integration of countries through goods, services, investment, technology and people.
Until mid-20th century production was mostly within countries; trade linked them.
MNCs own or control production in more than one nation, seeking markets, cheap labour, resources and friendly policies.
MNCs spread via joint production, buying local firms (Cargill–Parakh), and orders to small producers (garments, footwear, sports goods).
Ford Motors in Chennai (1995, with Mahindra) shows interlinked production and exports.
Foreign trade integrates markets: more choice, prices equalise, distant producers compete (Chinese toys).
Movement of people has grown little due to restrictions.
Technology — containers, cheaper transport, IT and internet — drives globalisation.
Liberalisation from 1991 removed India's trade and investment barriers, which had protected young industries.
WTO (1995) liberalises trade, but developed countries keep subsidies and barriers unfairly.
Well-off consumers, MNCs and top Indian firms gained; some Indian firms became MNCs; IT services grew; SEZs offer tax holidays.
Small producers (capacitors, toys, dairy, oil) suffered; work became temporary and 'flexible' (Sushila).
Fair globalisation needs labour-law enforcement, support for small producers, fair WTO rules and people's campaigns.

Money spent on assets such as land, buildings, machines
Investment made by MNCs in another country

Removal of barriers to trade and investment
World Trade Organisation, set up in 1995 to liberalise trade

rd-school-c10-social-c.e5-consumer-right.title: Consumer Rights
rd-school-c10-social-c.e5-consumer-right.subtitle: The short weight, the fake label, the bill that never adds up — and the law that lets you fight back

sections.h: A packet of biscuits and a big question

sections.md:
Markets need rules and regulations to protect consumers. Why? Because the individual consumer often finds herself in a **weak position**. Whenever there is a complaint regarding a good or service bought, the seller tries to shift all responsibility to the buyer. Their position usually is: "If you didn't like what you bought, please go elsewhere" — as if the seller has no responsibility once a sale is complete.

**Forms of exploitation in the market:**

- **Under-weighing and under-measurement** — 900 g sold as 1 kg; short petrol at a pump.
- **Overcharging** — charging more than the **Maximum Retail Price (MRP)**, e.g. ₹25 for a ₹20 bottle of water at a railway station.
- **Adulteration** — mixing cheaper substances: water in milk, brick powder in chilli powder, papaya seeds in black pepper. Edible oil adulteration has caused deaths.
- **Defective goods** — a mixer that stops working in a week.
- **Duplicate or fake goods** — fake medicines, look-alike brands.
- **False or incomplete information** — misleading advertisements, hidden side-effects, missing expiry dates.
- **Poor after-sales service** and harassment.

**Why are consumers weak?** Large companies with huge wealth, power and reach can manipulate the market in various ways. They use **attractive advertisements** through media to make us believe a product is good. For example, a company sold powder milk for babies as the best product, claiming it was better than mother's milk — it took years of struggle before the company was forced to accept it was making false claims. Similarly, a long battle had to be fought in courts to make **cigarette manufacturing companies** accept that their product could cause cancer.

Consumers buy in **small quantities**, are **scattered**, and are often unaware of their rights. Sellers are few and organised. Hence the need for rules — and for consumer awareness.

sections.md:
The consumer movement arose out of **dissatisfaction of consumers** as many unfair practices were being indulged in by sellers. There was no legal system available to consumers to protect them from exploitation. For a long time, when a consumer was not happy with a brand, she would simply stop buying it. It was presumed that it was the responsibility of consumers to be careful while buying — *caveat emptor*, 'let the buyer beware'.

It took many years for organisations in India and around the world to create awareness among people. This shifted the responsibility of ensuring quality of goods and services **on to the sellers**.

**In India**, the consumer movement as a 'social force' originated with the necessity of protecting and promoting the interests of consumers against unethical and unfair trade practices. **Rampant food shortages, hoarding, black marketing, adulteration of food and edible oil** gave birth to the movement in an organised form in the **1960s**. Till the 1970s, consumer organisations were largely engaged in writing articles and holding exhibitions. They formed consumer groups to look into the malpractices in ration shops and overcrowding in road passenger transport. More recently, India witnessed an upsurge in the number of consumer groups.

Because of all these efforts, the movement succeeded in bringing pressure on business firms as well as government to correct business conduct. A major step was taken in **1986** by the Indian government: the enactment of the **Consumer Protection Act, 1986**, popularly known as **COPRA**. (It has since been replaced by the **Consumer Protection Act, 2019**, which added e-commerce rules and a Central Consumer Protection Authority.)

**Internationally:** In **1985**, the **United Nations** adopted the **UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection**. This was a tool for nations to adopt measures to protect consumers and for consumer advocacy groups to press their governments to do so. At the international level, **Consumers International** (founded 1960 as the International Organisation of Consumers Unions) became an umbrella body of over 240 organisations from over 100 countries.

items.what: Organised consumer movement begins in India amid shortages, hoarding, adulteration
International Organisation of Consumers Unions (now Consumers International) founded
UN Guidelines for Consumer Protection adopted
Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) passed in India
Right to Information Act
New Consumer Protection Act replaces COPRA

sections.md:
While using many goods and services, we as consumers have the **right to be protected against the marketing of goods and delivery of services that are hazardous to life and property**. Producers need to strictly follow the required **safety rules and regulations**.

There are many goods and services that require special attention to safety: **pressure cookers** have a safety valve which, if defective, can cause a serious accident; **electrical appliances**, **medicines**, **LPG cylinders**, **cars**, and even **construction of buildings**. The manufacturers of the safety valve have to ensure high quality. You also need public or government action to see that this quality is maintained. However, we do find bad-quality products in the market because supervision of these rules is weak and the consumer movement is not strong enough.

**Case (retold): Reji Mathew.** Reji Mathew was a healthy boy studying in Class 9 in a school in Kerala. He developed pain in his throat and his father took him to a private clinic. The doctor advised removal of his tonsils. In the hospital an **anaesthetist** — who was not properly qualified — gave him the anaesthesia. After the operation Reji showed symptoms of abnormality; investigations found he had suffered **brain damage** and could not stand properly. His father filed a complaint in the **State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission**, alleging medical negligence. The hospital denied it. After a long hearing with medical evidence, the Commission held the hospital responsible for negligence and directed it to pay **compensation**.

Which right was violated? The **right to safety** — a medical service must not endanger the patient's life. The case also shows the **right to seek redressal** being used.

check.q: A pressure cooker whose safety valve bursts violates which right?
check.why: Goods hazardous to life and property breach the consumer's right to safety.

sections.md:
When you buy a commodity, you find certain details printed on the packing: **ingredients, price, batch number, date of manufacture, expiry date, and the address of the manufacturer**. When we buy medicines, we find 'directions for proper use' and information about **side effects and risks**. When you buy garments, you find 'instructions for washing'.

Why? Because consumers have the **right to be informed** about the particulars of goods and services they purchase. Consumers can then complain and ask for compensation or replacement if the product proves defective. For example, if we buy a product and find it defective well within the expiry period, we can ask for a replacement. If the expiry period was not printed, the manufacturer would blame the shopkeeper and would not accept responsibility. If people sell medicines that have expired, action can be taken against them. Similarly, one can protest and complain if someone sells a good at more than the printed price — the **MRP**. Consumers can bargain with the seller to sell at less than MRP.

**Right to Information Act (RTI), 2005.** In October 2005, the Government of India enacted a law popularly known as the RTI Act, which ensures citizens all the information about the **functions of government departments**.

**Case (retold): Amritlal's question.** An engineering graduate, after submitting all certificates and attending an interview for a job in a government department, received no news of the result. Officials would not give a satisfactory answer. He filed an application under the RTI Act asking for the result in a reasonable time, and also the reasons for the delay, names of selected candidates and the marks obtained. Under the Act he received the information — and soon got his appointment letter. RTI extended the right to be informed from the market to governance.

check.q: The RTI Act (2005) gives citizens the right to information about…
check.why: RTI makes government departments answerable to citizens' requests for information.

sections.md:
Any consumer who receives a service, in whatever capacity, regardless of age, gender and nature of service, has the **right to choose** whether to continue to receive the service.

Suppose you want to buy toothpaste, and the shop owner says she can sell the toothpaste only if you buy a toothbrush too. If you are not interested in the brush, your right to choice is denied. Similarly, sometimes gas supply dealers insist that you buy a gas stove from them when you take a new connection. In this way you are often forced to buy things that you may not wish to, and you are left with no choice.

The right to choose also means a **variety of goods at competitive prices** should be available. Monopolies — where one seller controls the market — weaken this right.

**Case (retold): Abhiram's phone bill.** A man (the textbook's example) paid his landline/mobile bills regularly, but one month the bill showed a huge amount for calls he never made. When he complained, the company asked him to pay first and argue later. He refused and approached the **District Consumer Commission**, arguing the bill was wrong and that he was being forced to pay for a service he had not used. The commission examined the call records, found the billing faulty, and ordered the company to correct the bill and pay him compensation for harassment. This involves both the **right to information** (an itemised bill) and the **right to seek redressal**.

check.q: A gas dealer refusing a new connection unless you buy his stove denies your…
check.why: Tying one purchase to another removes the consumer's freedom to choose.

sections.h: Where should consumers go? Right to seek redressal
sections.md:
Consumers have the **right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices and exploitation**. If any damage is done to a consumer, she has the right to get **compensation** depending on the degree of damage. There is a need to provide an easy and effective public system by which this can be done.

**Case (retold): Prakash and the fee refund.** A student — call him Prakash — took admission in a private institute for a course and paid the full year's fees in advance. A month later, he got admission into a government college and wanted to withdraw. The institute refused to refund any money. Prakash complained to the **District Consumer Commission**. It ruled that the institute could keep only a reasonable amount and must refund the rest of the fees — a service not delivered cannot be charged for in full.

**Consumer courts (three-tier quasi-judicial machinery).** Under COPRA, a three-tier system was set up at the **district, state and national levels**:

| Level | Body | Claims handled (Consumer Protection Act 2019, as revised 2021) |
|---|---|---|
| District | District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission | up to ₹1 crore |
| State | State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission | ₹1 crore – ₹10 crore |
| National | National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (New Delhi) | above ₹10 crore |

*(Older textbooks give COPRA 1986 limits: district up to ₹20 lakh, state ₹20 lakh–₹1 crore, national above ₹1 crore. Use whichever figures your syllabus asks for.)*

If a case is dismissed at district level, the consumer can **appeal** in the state, and then the national commission. A consumer **does not need a lawyer** — she can represent herself. Complaints can now also be filed online (e-Daakhil portal). The textbook also calls these courts **consumer forums**.

sections.h: Right to represent and consumer education
sections.md:
The Act has enabled us as consumers to have the **right to represent in the consumer courts**. Consumers also have a right to be heard — their interests must receive due consideration at appropriate forums.

**Consumer protection councils / consumer groups.** In India, consumer movement groups are known as **consumer forums or consumer protection councils**. They **guide consumers on how to file cases** in the consumer court. On many occasions they also **represent individual consumers** in the consumer courts. These voluntary organisations also receive financial support from the government for creating awareness among people. If you walk into a residential colony you may notice resident welfare associations (RWAs) — if there is any unfair trade practice against their members, they act on their behalf.

Today there are **more than 700 consumer groups** in the country, of which only about 20–25 are well organised and recognised for their work.

**Right to consumer education.** The consumer has the right to acquire the knowledge and skill to be an informed consumer throughout life. Awareness campaigns such as **'Jago Grahak Jago'** (Wake up, consumer) by the Government of India spread this knowledge on TV, radio and posters.

**Consumer responsibilities.** Rights come with duties:

- Ask for a **cash memo / bill** for every purchase — it is your proof.
- Check **ISI/Agmark/Hallmark** marks, MRP, expiry date.
- Read labels and warranty terms.
- File genuine complaints and do not make false claims.
- Form or join consumer groups.
- Be environmentally responsible — avoid waste.
keyTerms: Consumer forum — voluntary group guiding and representing consumers
Jago Grahak Jago — government awareness campaign
Cash memo — bill that proves a purchase

check.q: Why is a cash memo important for a consumer?
options: It is proof of purchase needed to file a complaint
It is required to pay GST
check.why: Without proof of purchase it is hard to establish a claim in a consumer court.

sections.md:
When we as consumers become conscious of our rights while purchasing various goods and services, we are able to discriminate and make informed choices. This calls for acquiring the knowledge and skill to become a well-informed consumer.

**Standardisation marks.** While buying many commodities, on the cover you might have seen a logo with the letters **ISI**, **Agmark** or **Hallmark**. These logos and certification help consumers get assured of quality while purchasing goods and services. The organisations that monitor and issue these certificates allow producers to use their logos provided they follow certain quality standards.

| Mark | Used for | Given by |
|---|---|---|
| **ISI** | Industrial and consumer goods: electrical appliances, cement, LPG cylinders, helmets | Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) |
| **Agmark** | Agricultural products: ghee, honey, pulses, spices, edible oil | Directorate of Marketing & Inspection |
| **Hallmark** | Purity of gold and silver jewellery | BIS |

Though these organisations develop standards for many products, it is not compulsory for all producers to follow standards. However, for some products that affect the health and safety of consumers or are of mass consumption — like **LPG cylinders, food colours and additives, cement, packaged drinking water** — it is **mandatory** for producers to get certified. (Since 2021, hallmarking of gold jewellery is also mandatory in most districts.)

**International standards.** The **International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO)**, Geneva, sets standards accepted worldwide; **Codex Alimentarius** (FAO/WHO) sets food standards.

**Did you know?** The 'Veg' green dot and 'Non-veg' brown dot on food packets are also mandatory labels in India — another form of the right to information.

sections.md:
India has been observing **24 December** as the **National Consumer Day**. It was on this day that the Indian Parliament enacted the Consumer Protection Act in **1986**. (**15 March** is World Consumer Rights Day.)

The consumer movement in India has made some progress in terms of numbers of organised groups and their activities. But the textbook is honest about its limits:

- The consumer redressal process is becoming **cumbersome, expensive and time-consuming**. In many cases consumers are required to engage lawyers. Cases require time for filing, attending court proceedings etc.
- In most purchases **cash memos are not issued**, so evidence is not easy to gather.
- Most purchases in the market are **small retail sales**.
- The existing laws are **not very clear on compensation** to consumers injured by defective products.
- More than 35 years after the enactment of COPRA, consumer awareness is spreading but slowly; the **enforcement of laws** that protect workers, especially in the unorganised sectors, is weak; rules and regulations for working of markets are often not followed.

The way forward is **voluntary effort and active participation** by consumers themselves. The consumer movement can be effective only with the active involvement of consumers. It requires a voluntary effort and struggle involving the participation of one and all.

**New since the book was written:** the Consumer Protection Act 2019 created a **Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA)** to act against misleading advertisements (including celebrity endorsers), unfair trade practices and unsafe products; brought **e-commerce platforms** under consumer law; introduced **product liability**; and allowed complaints to be filed where the consumer lives, and online. The **National Consumer Helpline is 1915**.

check.q: National Consumer Day in India is observed on…
check.why: Parliament enacted the Consumer Protection Act on 24 December 1986, so that day is National Consumer Day.

story.title: The Case of the Shrinking Ghee

parts.md: Meera, sixteen, from Jaipur, was helping her mother make laddoos for Diwali when she noticed something odd. The 1-litre tin of ghee they had bought from a new brand was strangely light. On the kitchen scale it weighed far less than the printed net quantity. The smell was wrong too. There was no Agmark logo — only a shiny picture of a cow. Her mother shrugged: "What can we do? Throw it away." Meera had just read Chapter 5. She kept the tin, the bill (luckily the shop had given one) and took photos.

She called the National Consumer Helpline, 1915, which guided her to file on the e-Daakhil portal. The claim — refund plus ₹5,000 for harassment — was far under ₹1 crore, so it went to the District Commission. No lawyer needed. A local consumer forum volunteer helped her write the complaint: violation of the right to information (false quantity), the right to safety (possible adulteration) and the right to seek redressal. Months later the commission ordered the seller and the brand to refund the price, pay compensation and costs. The brand pulled the batch. Meera's mother framed the order next to the family photos. "Jago Grahak Jago," she said, laughing.

summary: We are all consumers of goods and services; individual consumers are in a weak position against powerful sellers.
Exploitation: under-weighing, overcharging above MRP, adulteration, defective and duplicate goods, false information, poor service.
Big firms can mislead through advertising (baby milk powder, cigarettes cases).
The consumer movement arose from dissatisfaction; in India it organised in the 1960s against shortages, hoarding, adulteration.
Responsibility shifted from 'buyer beware' to sellers ensuring quality.
COPRA 1986 (now Consumer Protection Act 2019); UN Guidelines 1985; Consumers International.
Right to safety — Reji Mathew's medical negligence case.
Right to be informed — labels, MRP, expiry; RTI Act 2005 extends it to government.
Right to choose — no forced tie-in purchases.
Right to seek redressal — three-tier District, State, National commissions; no lawyer required.
Right to represent and consumer education; consumer forums guide and represent consumers; 'Jago Grahak Jago'.
Standard marks: ISI and Hallmark (BIS), Agmark; mandatory for some products like LPG cylinders and food colours.

rd-school-c11-accountancy-a.ch01-introdu.title: Introduction to Accounting
rd-school-c11-accountancy-a.ch01-introdu.subtitle: Every business, from a chai stall to Tata Steel, speaks one language — the language of accounts

sections.h: Ramesh's chai stall: why keep accounts?

sections.md:
Every organisation — business or not — needs information about its economic activities. The **American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA)** in **1941** defined accounting as:

> the art of recording, classifying, and summarising in a significant manner and in terms of money, transactions and events which are, in part at least, of financial character, and interpreting the results thereof.

In **1966**, the **American Accounting Association (AAA)** gave a wider definition: accounting is *the process of identifying, measuring and communicating economic information to permit informed judgements and decisions by users of the information.*

From these we can list the **attributes (steps) of accounting**:

1. **Economic events** — accounting deals with events involving financial character (buying a machine, selling goods, paying salaries). Events that cannot be measured in money (the manager's honesty, a strike threat) are not recorded.
2. **Identification** — deciding which transactions should be recorded, i.e. which are financial in nature.
3. **Measurement** — quantifying the events in **money terms** (₹), the common unit.
4. **Recording** — writing them in the books of account in chronological order (Journal).
5. **Classifying** — grouping transactions of similar nature in one place (Ledger accounts).
6. **Summarising** — preparing the **Trial Balance**, **Profit and Loss Account** and **Balance Sheet** in a manner useful to users.
7. **Analysing and interpreting** — drawing meaning from the summary (is profit rising? can debts be paid?).
8. **Communicating** — sending the information to users in the form of reports, timely and regularly.

**Bookkeeping vs accounting.** **Bookkeeping** is the recording phase — identifying, measuring, recording and classifying. It is routine and clerical. **Accounting** goes further: summarising, analysing, interpreting and communicating. **Accountancy** is the whole body of knowledge (the subject you are studying).

sections.h: Accounting as a source of information
sections.md:
Accounting is the means of communicating information about a business to those who need it. The system works as an **information system**: it collects and processes data and gives useful reports.

The information generated can be grouped as:

- **Information relating to profit or loss** — through the Income Statement (Profit and Loss Account);
- **Information relating to financial position** — assets, liabilities, capital through the Balance Sheet;
- **Information relating to cash flow** — where cash came from and where it went;
- **Management information** — costs of products, budgets, departmental results — for internal decisions.

Accounting information is presented in the form of **financial statements**, which are the end products of the accounting process.

**Users of accounting information.** There are two broad groups:

| Internal users | What they want |
|---|---|
| Owners / shareholders | Profit earned, safety of capital |
| Management | Information for planning, control and decisions |
| Employees and workers | Profits (for bonus), stability of employment |

| External users | What they want |
|---|---|
| Banks and financial institutions | Ability to repay loans with interest |
| Investors and potential investors | Profitability and future prospects |
| Creditors and suppliers | Short-term solvency — will they be paid on time? |
| Government and tax authorities | Tax due (income tax, GST), policy decisions |
| Researchers, consumers and the public | Performance, social responsibility, product pricing |

Note: some books list employees as external users. NCERT treats owners, management and employees as internal users.

check.q: A bank deciding whether to lend to a firm is mainly interested in…
options: The firm's ability to repay with interest
check.why: Lenders, as external users, care about solvency and repayment capacity.

sections.md:
Information is useful only if it has certain qualities. NCERT lists four:

1. **Reliability** — users must be able to depend on it. It should be **verifiable** (backed by vouchers such as bills and receipts), **free from error and bias**, and **faithfully represent** what it claims to represent. If Ramesh writes ₹8,000 as sales when actual sales were ₹6,000, the information is unreliable.
2. **Relevance** — information must be **available in time**, help in prediction and feedback, and **influence decisions**. Last year's figures delivered two years late are not relevant.
3. **Understandability** — decision makers must interpret it in the same sense as the preparer. Information should be presented in a way that a user with reasonable knowledge of business can understand; technical jargon should be explained.
4. **Comparability** — users should be able to compare figures **over time (intra-firm)** and **across firms (inter-firm)**. This requires consistent methods and a common unit of measurement and format.

Sometimes these conflict: very timely (relevant) information may be less verified (reliable). Accountants try to balance them.

**Did you know?** The qualitative characteristics used by NCERT come from conceptual frameworks such as those of the International Accounting Standards Board, which also speaks of 'faithful representation' and 'timeliness'.
