rd-school-c11-accountancy-b.ch07-depreci.title: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
rd-school-c11-accountancy-b.ch07-depreci.subtitle: Why a ₹10 lakh delivery truck quietly loses value every year — and how accountants plan for bad days

sections.md:
**Depreciation** is a **decline in the value of a fixed asset** due to use, passage of time or obsolescence. In accounting, it is the **allocation of the depreciable cost of an asset** over its **useful life** in a systematic and rational manner. ICAI's standard described it as a measure of the wearing out, consumption or other loss of value of a depreciable asset.

**Features:**

1. It is a **decline in the book value** of fixed assets (not current assets).
2. It includes loss of value due to **use, passage of time or obsolescence**.
3. It is a **continuing process** till the end of the asset's useful life.
4. It is an **expired cost** and must be deducted before calculating taxable profit.
5. It is a **non-cash expense** — no cash goes out when depreciation is charged.

**Related terms:**

- **Depletion** — used for **natural resources (wasting assets)** like mines, quarries, oil wells. The value falls as material is extracted. Usually computed on the basis of quantity extracted: (cost ÷ total estimated quantity) × quantity extracted this year.
- **Amortisation** — writing off the cost of **intangible assets** such as patents, copyrights, trademarks, franchises, goodwill over their useful life.

| Asset type | Term |
|---|---|
| Tangible fixed asset (machine, building, van) | Depreciation |
| Natural resource (coal mine) | Depletion |
| Intangible (patent, software licence) | Amortisation |

Land is generally **not depreciated** because it has an unlimited life (unless it is a mine or quarry).

check.q: Writing off the cost of a patent over its life is called…
check.why: Intangible assets like patents are amortised; depletion is for natural resources.

sections.md:
**Causes of depreciation:**

1. **Wear and tear due to use or passage of time.** Physical deterioration — a van's engine and tyres wear out; buildings weather.
2. **Expiration of legal rights.** Assets like patents, copyrights and leases lose value as the legal period expires — a 10-year lease loses one-tenth each year.
3. **Obsolescence.** An asset becomes outdated because of new technology, changed demand or new inventions — e.g. CRT monitors replaced by LED screens, feature phones by smartphones, even if they still work.
4. **Abnormal factors.** Accidents, fire, earthquake, flood — decline in value due to such events (these are usually treated as losses, not regular depreciation).

**Need for depreciation:**

1. **Matching of costs and revenue.** An asset helps earn revenue over many years; part of its cost must be charged each year against that revenue (matching concept).
2. **Consideration of tax.** Depreciation is a deductible expense under the Income-tax Act; it reduces taxable profit. (Tax depreciation rules may differ from book depreciation.)
3. **True and fair financial position.** Assets must be shown at their reduced (book) value in the Balance Sheet, not at original cost.
4. **Compliance with law.** The Companies Act 2013 (Schedule II) requires companies to charge depreciation.
5. **Replacement of assets.** Charging depreciation reduces profit available for distribution, retaining funds that help replace the asset at the end of its life.

check.q: A working CRT computer monitor replaced by a newer LED model loses value mainly due to…
check.why: It is outdated by new technology even though it still works — that is obsolescence.

sections.md:
Three factors decide the amount of depreciation:

1. **Cost of the asset** — purchase price plus freight, transport, installation, commissioning, trial runs, legal costs and any other expenditure to bring it to a usable condition. GST paid on an asset is part of cost only if input tax credit is not available. **Example:** machine price ₹4,60,000 + freight ₹15,000 + installation ₹25,000 = **₹5,00,000**.
2. **Estimated net residual value (scrap value)** — the net amount the business expects to get when the asset is disposed of at the end of its life, after deducting disposal costs.
3. **Depreciable cost** = cost − net residual value.
4. **Estimated useful life** — the period over which the asset is expected to be used by the enterprise (in years, or units such as hours or km). It is usually shorter than physical life, because of obsolescence and the firm's replacement policy.

Depreciation is thus based on **estimates** — residual value and useful life are judgements, revised when needed.

check.q: A machine costs ₹2,40,000 with installation ₹10,000; scrap value ₹25,000. Depreciable cost is…

sections.md:
Under the **Straight Line Method** (fixed instalment / original cost method), a **fixed amount** is charged as depreciation every year over the useful life.

> Annual depreciation = (Cost − Net residual value) ÷ Useful life

> Rate of depreciation (%) = Annual depreciation ÷ Cost × 100

**Example:** Van cost ₹5,00,000, residual value ₹50,000, life 5 years. Depreciation = (5,00,000 − 50,000) ÷ 5 = **₹90,000 per year**; rate = 90,000 ÷ 5,00,000 × 100 = **18%**.

| Year | Opening book value | Depreciation | Closing book value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5,00,000 | 90,000 | 4,10,000 |
| 2 | 4,10,000 | 90,000 | 3,20,000 |
| 3 | 3,20,000 | 90,000 | 2,30,000 |
| 4 | 2,30,000 | 90,000 | 1,40,000 |
| 5 | 1,40,000 | 90,000 | 50,000 |

Plotted on a graph, the book value falls in a **straight line** — hence the name.

**Part-year purchases:** if bought on 1 October and accounts close on 31 March, charge for 6 months: 90,000 × 6/12 = ₹45,000.

**Advantages:** simple to calculate and understand; asset can be written down to exactly scrap value; useful where the asset's utility is uniform (leases, patents, furniture).
**Limitations:** ignores the fact that repairs rise as the asset ages, so total charge (depreciation + repairs) rises over time; the depreciation charge does not fall even when efficiency falls; not accepted by income-tax law for most assets (WDV is used for tax in India).

sections.md:
Under the **Written Down Value Method** (reducing / diminishing balance method), depreciation is charged at a **fixed rate on the reducing book value** (written down value) each year. So the amount of depreciation **falls every year**.

**Example:** Van cost ₹5,00,000, WDV rate 20%.

| Year | Opening WDV | Depreciation 20% | Closing WDV |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5,00,000 | 1,00,000 | 4,00,000 |
| 2 | 4,00,000 | 80,000 | 3,20,000 |
| 3 | 3,20,000 | 64,000 | 2,56,000 |
| 4 | 2,56,000 | 51,200 | 2,04,800 |
| 5 | 2,04,800 | 40,960 | 1,63,840 |

The book value **never becomes zero**.

**Advantages:** depreciation is high in early years when repairs are low, and low in later years when repairs are high — so the **total charge (depreciation + repairs) stays roughly even**; it is **accepted by income-tax authorities** in India; it suits assets that face obsolescence and lose value faster early on (computers, vehicles, plant).
**Limitations:** the asset can never be fully written off; calculating the right rate is harder; the method is a little more complex.

**Comparison of SLM and WDV:**

| Basis | SLM | WDV |
|---|---|---|
| Basis of calculation | Original cost | Book value (reducing) |
| Annual charge | Fixed every year | Decreases every year |
| Book value at end | Can become zero / scrap value | Never zero |
| Total charge with repairs | Rises in later years | Roughly uniform |
| Income tax | Generally not accepted | Accepted |
| Suitable for | Patents, leases, furniture | Plant, machinery, vehicles, computers |

check.q: Under WDV at 10%, an asset of ₹50,000: depreciation in year 2 is…

sections.md:
**Method 1 — Charging depreciation to the asset account.** Depreciation is credited to the asset account each year, reducing its balance.

- Purchase: Asset A/c Dr; To Bank A/c.
- Charging: **Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c.**
- Closing: **Profit and Loss A/c Dr; To Depreciation A/c.**

The asset appears in the Balance Sheet at its **written down value**. The original cost is not visible.

**Method 2 — Creating a Provision for Depreciation (Accumulated Depreciation) Account.** The asset account continues to show **original cost**; depreciation is accumulated in a separate account with a credit balance.

- Charging: **Depreciation A/c Dr; To Provision for Depreciation A/c.**
- Closing: **Profit and Loss A/c Dr; To Depreciation A/c.**
- In the Balance Sheet: Asset at cost **less** accumulated depreciation = net book value.

Advantages of Method 2: original cost and total depreciation are both visible; required by the Companies Act formats; easy to find profit or loss on sale.

**Example (SLM ₹90,000 p.a. on the ₹5,00,000 van, Method 2):** after 3 years, Van A/c = ₹5,00,000 (debit), Provision for Depreciation A/c = ₹2,70,000 (credit), net book value ₹2,30,000 — same as the SLM table.

check.q: Under the provision for depreciation method, the asset account shows…
check.why: Depreciation accumulates in a separate provision account, so the asset account keeps its original cost.

sections.md:
When an asset is sold or scrapped, its book value is compared with the sale proceeds. **Profit or loss on sale** = Sale price − Book value on the date of sale (after charging depreciation up to that date).

**Method 1 (asset account method):**

1. Charge depreciation up to date of sale: Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset A/c.
2. Record sale: Bank A/c Dr; To Asset A/c.
3. Profit: Asset A/c Dr; To Profit and Loss A/c. Loss: Profit and Loss A/c Dr; To Asset A/c.

**Method 2 (with provision) — Asset Disposal Account:**

1. Transfer cost: **Asset Disposal A/c Dr; To Asset A/c** (original cost).
2. Transfer accumulated depreciation: **Provision for Depreciation A/c Dr; To Asset Disposal A/c.**
3. Sale proceeds: **Bank A/c Dr; To Asset Disposal A/c.**
4. Balance = profit (credit) or loss (debit), transferred to P&L A/c.

**Example:** Machine bought 1 April 2023 for ₹1,00,000; SLM ₹18,000 a year (scrap ₹10,000, life 5 years); sold on 30 September 2025 for ₹50,000. Depreciation: 2023–24 ₹18,000; 2024–25 ₹18,000; 1 April–30 Sept 2025 ₹9,000 (6 months) → total ₹45,000. Book value = 1,00,000 − 45,000 = ₹55,000. **Loss** = 55,000 − 50,000 = **₹5,000**.

**Additions and extensions.** Expenditure that **increases capacity or life** of an asset (adding a new floor, upgrading a machine) is **capital expenditure** and is added to the asset's cost, then depreciated over its remaining life. Routine **repairs** are revenue expenses.

**Did you know?** Schedule II of the Companies Act 2013 gives **useful lives** (e.g. general furniture 10 years, computers 3 years, motor cars 8 years) instead of fixed rates.

check.q: Book value of an asset on date of sale ₹40,000; sold for ₹46,000. Result?
check.why: Sale price exceeds book value by ₹6,000, which is a profit on sale credited to P&L.

sections.md:
A **provision** is an amount **charged against profit** to provide for a **known liability or expected loss whose amount cannot be determined with substantial accuracy**. NCERT's examples: provision for **depreciation**, provision for **bad and doubtful debts**, provision for **taxation**, provision for **discount on debtors**, provision for **repairs and renewals**.

Provisions follow the **prudence (conservatism)** concept: provide for all possible losses.

**Accounting:** Profit and Loss A/c Dr; To Provision A/c. In the Balance Sheet, provisions are either deducted from the related asset (doubtful debts from debtors; depreciation from asset) or shown on the liabilities side (provision for tax).

**Provision for doubtful debts — example.** Debtors on 31 March ₹50,000. Further bad debts to be written off ₹2,000. Provision for doubtful debts to be made at 5%.

- Bad debts: Bad Debts A/c Dr 2,000; To Debtors 2,000.
- Remaining debtors = 48,000; provision = 5% × 48,000 = **₹2,400**: P&L A/c Dr 2,400; To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c 2,400.
- Balance Sheet: Debtors 48,000 less provision 2,400 = **₹45,600**.

If an old provision exists, only the **difference** (new provision + bad debts − old provision) is charged to P&L.

**Importance:** gives true profit and true value of assets; prevents overstatement of profit; follows prudence.

check.q: Debtors ₹80,000; provision required 5%. Amount of provision?

sections.md:
A **reserve** is a part of **profit set aside** (appropriated) to **strengthen the financial position** and meet unknown future needs. It is **not** a charge against profit; it is an **appropriation of profit**. It is shown on the liabilities side under **Reserves and Surplus** (with capital).

**Accounting:** Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr; To Reserve A/c.

**Types of reserves:**

1. **Revenue reserves** — created from **revenue profits** from normal operations.
   - **General reserve** — not created for any specific purpose; strengthens financial position, meets contingencies.
   - **Specific reserves** — for a stated purpose: **Dividend Equalisation Reserve** (to keep dividend stable), **Workmen Compensation Reserve**, **Investment Fluctuation Reserve**, **Debenture Redemption Reserve**.
2. **Capital reserves** — created from **capital profits** not arising from normal operations: premium on issue of shares or debentures, profit on sale of fixed assets, profit on reissue of forfeited shares, profit on revaluation of assets and liabilities, profit prior to incorporation, profit on redemption of debentures. Capital reserves are generally **not available for distribution as dividend** (they can be used to write off capital losses or issue bonus shares).
3. **Secret reserve** — a reserve **not disclosed** in the Balance Sheet, created by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities, or charging excessive depreciation. It may reduce taxes or hide profits from competitors, but it reduces transparency, and companies are not permitted to create secret reserves under the Companies Act.

**Reserve vs Reserve Fund:** when the amount of a reserve is invested outside the business (in securities), it is called a **reserve fund**.

**Provisions vs Reserves:**

| Basis | Provision | Reserve |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Charge against profit | Appropriation of profit |
| Purpose | Known liability or expected loss | Strengthen position; future needs |
| Effect on profit | Created even if there is a loss | Created only from profit |
| Balance Sheet | Deducted from asset or shown as liability | Under Reserves and Surplus |
| Dividend | Cannot be used | Revenue reserve can be used |
| Legal need | Must be created (prudence) | Generally at discretion, sometimes required |

summary: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of depreciable cost of a fixed asset over its useful life.
It is a decline in book value, continuous, a non-cash expense.
Depletion is for natural resources; amortisation for intangibles.
Causes: wear and tear, expiry of legal rights, obsolescence, abnormal factors.
Need: matching, tax, true financial position, legal compliance, funds for replacement.
Factors: cost (including installation), residual value, useful life.
SLM: fixed charge = (cost − scrap) ÷ life; book value falls in a straight line.
WDV: fixed rate on reducing balance; charge falls each year; accepted for tax; never zero.
Recording: charge to asset A/c, or accumulate in Provision for Depreciation A/c (asset at cost).
Disposal: profit/loss = sale price − book value at date of sale; Asset Disposal A/c.
Additions that increase capacity are capitalised; repairs are revenue.
Provisions are charges against profit for known liabilities or expected losses (doubtful debts, tax).
Reserves are appropriations of profit: revenue (general, specific), capital, secret.
Capital reserves come from capital profits and are generally not distributable.
Provisions reduce profit; reserves are set aside from profit.

rd-school-c11-accountancy-b.ch08-financi.subtitle: A year of business on two pages: the Trading and Profit & Loss Account and the Balance Sheet

sections.md:
**Stakeholders** are people or groups interested in a business's financial results:

| Stakeholder | Main information need |
|---|---|
| **Owners / investors** | Profit, return on capital, safety of investment |
| **Management** | Performance of departments, costs, decisions on pricing and expansion |
| **Creditors and suppliers** | Short-term ability to pay (liquidity) |
| **Lenders (banks)** | Long-term solvency, ability to pay interest and repay loans |
| **Employees** | Profitability for bonus, stability of jobs |
| **Government and tax authorities** | Correct tax (income tax, GST), economic statistics |
| **Customers** | Continuity of supply, after-sales service |
| **Public and researchers** | Social responsibility, employment, environment |

The **Trading and P&L Account** answers profitability questions; the **Balance Sheet** answers financial position questions. Together they are called **final accounts** for sole proprietors; for companies they are the Statement of Profit and Loss and Balance Sheet under Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013.

check.q: A supplier giving goods on 30 days' credit is most interested in…
check.why: Creditors want to know whether the business can pay its short-term dues on time.

sections.md:
Before preparing statements we must separate **capital** items (go to the Balance Sheet) from **revenue** items (go to the Trading and P&L Account).

**Capital expenditure** — benefits the business for **more than one accounting year**; is incurred to acquire, extend or improve fixed assets; is **non-recurring**; increases earning capacity. Examples: purchase of land, building, machinery, furniture, vehicles; cost of installation, freight on a new machine; legal charges on buying property; addition to a building; heavy overhaul that extends life. Shown in the **Balance Sheet** as assets.

**Revenue expenditure** — benefits only the **current year**; is incurred for day-to-day running; is **recurring**; maintains earning capacity. Examples: purchase of goods, wages, salaries, rent, electricity, repairs and maintenance, carriage, advertisement, depreciation, interest on loan. Charged to the **Trading and P&L Account**.

**Deferred revenue expenditure** — revenue in nature but benefit spread over several years, so written off over a few years: heavy advertisement to launch a new product, large research costs. (Under current standards most such costs are expensed; know the concept.)

**Capital receipts** — non-recurring receipts that create a liability or reduce an asset: capital introduced, loans raised, sale proceeds of fixed assets. Shown in the Balance Sheet (except any profit on sale, which goes to P&L).

**Revenue receipts** — recurring receipts from normal operations: sales, commission, interest, rent, dividend received, discount received. Go to the Trading and P&L Account.

**Why it matters:** if capital expenditure is wrongly treated as revenue, profit is **understated** and assets understated; if revenue is treated as capital, profit is **overstated**.

sections.md:
**Financial statements** are the statements showing the **profit or loss** of a period and the **financial position** at the end of it. For a sole proprietor they are:

1. **Trading and Profit and Loss Account** (Income Statement) — for the year ended 31 March;
2. **Balance Sheet** (Position Statement) — as at 31 March.

**Objectives:**

- **To present a true and fair view of the financial performance** — the profit or loss earned during the period.
- **To present a true and fair view of the financial position** — assets, liabilities and capital on a date.
- **To provide information to users** for decisions (lending, investing, taxing).
- **To help management** in planning and control; to enable comparison with past years and other firms.
- To meet **legal requirements** (tax returns, Companies Act).

The Trading and P&L Account is prepared for a **period** (like a video of the year); the Balance Sheet is on a **date** (like a photograph).

check.q: The Balance Sheet is prepared…
options: Only when there is a loss
check.why: It shows the position — assets, liabilities, capital — at one point of time.

sections.h: The Trading Account and gross profit
sections.md:
The **Trading Account** shows the result of **buying and selling goods** (and manufacturing, if any). Its balance is **Gross Profit** (credit side bigger) or **Gross Loss**.

**Format:**

*Trading Account of Anita Stationers for the year ended 31 March 2026*

| Dr. Particulars | ₹ | Cr. Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| To Opening stock | | By Sales | |
| To Purchases | | Less: Sales return | |
| Less: Purchases return | | By Closing stock | |
| To Direct expenses: wages, carriage inwards, freight, octroi, import duty, fuel/power, royalty on production, gas & water for factory | | | |
| To Gross profit c/d (balancing figure) | | | |

**Items explained:**

- **Opening stock** — unsold goods from last year (comes from the trial balance).
- **Purchases less returns outward** = net purchases. Goods withdrawn by owner, given as charity or samples are deducted from purchases.
- **Direct expenses** — incurred in buying goods and bringing them to the place of business or in production: **carriage/freight inwards, wages, cartage, customs/import duty, dock dues, power, factory lighting, royalty based on production**.
- **Sales less returns inward** = net sales (revenue from operations). Sale of old assets is **not** included.
- **Closing stock** — goods unsold at year end, valued at **cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower**; it is usually given **outside** the trial balance as an adjustment.

**Gross profit = Net sales − Cost of goods sold**, where **Cost of goods sold (COGS) = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock**.

**Did you know?** 'Wages and salaries' together are treated as a direct expense (Trading A/c) in NCERT problems, while 'salaries and wages' are often taken to the P&L Account — read the wording carefully, and state your assumption.

check.q: Carriage inwards is debited to the…
check.why: It is a direct cost of bringing purchased goods to the business, so it goes to the Trading Account.

sections.h: The Profit and Loss Account and net profit
sections.md:
The **Profit and Loss Account** starts with gross profit and records all **indirect expenses and losses** (debit) and **other incomes and gains** (credit). Its balance is **Net Profit** (or Net Loss), transferred to **Capital A/c**.

**Format:**

| Dr. Particulars | ₹ | Cr. Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| To Gross loss b/d (if any) | | By Gross profit b/d | |
| To Office & administration expenses: salaries, office rent, rates and taxes, printing & stationery, postage, telephone, insurance, audit fees, legal charges, office lighting | | By Other incomes: commission received, discount received, rent received, interest received, dividend received, bad debts recovered, profit on sale of assets | |
| To Selling & distribution expenses: advertisement, carriage outwards, salesmen's commission and salary, discount allowed, bad debts, packing, delivery van expenses, warehouse rent | | | |
| To Financial expenses: interest on loan, bank charges | | | |
| To Depreciation, repairs, loss by fire/theft, loss on sale of assets | | | |
| To Net profit (transferred to capital) | | | |

**Net profit = Gross profit + Other incomes − Indirect expenses and losses.**

**Operating profit.** NCERT also introduces **operating profit (EBIT-style)**: the profit from the **normal operations** of the business, *before* considering non-operating items. Operating profit = Net profit + non-operating expenses/losses (e.g. interest on loan, loss by fire, loss on sale of assets) − non-operating incomes (e.g. interest/dividend on investments, profit on sale of assets). It shows how well the core business performs.

**Closing entries.** At year end, nominal accounts are closed:

- Trading A/c Dr; To Opening Stock, Purchases, Sales Return, Wages, Carriage Inwards A/cs.
- Sales A/c Dr; Purchases Return A/c Dr; To Trading A/c.
- Closing Stock A/c Dr; To Trading A/c.
- Trading A/c Dr; To P&L A/c (gross profit).
- P&L A/c Dr; To expense/loss A/cs. Income A/cs Dr; To P&L A/c.
- P&L A/c Dr; To Capital A/c (net profit). Capital A/c Dr; To Drawings A/c.

**Opening entry** next year brings back asset, liability and capital balances (Chapter 3).

check.q: Carriage outwards is shown in the…
check.why: Carriage on goods sent to customers is a selling expense, an indirect cost charged to the P&L Account.

sections.h: The Balance Sheet: grouping and marshalling
sections.md:
The **Balance Sheet** is a **statement** (not an account) showing assets on one side and liabilities and capital on the other, as at a date. It is based on **A = L + C**.

**Grouping** — putting items of a similar nature under one head: e.g. 'Current assets' include cash, bank, debtors, bills receivable, stock, prepaid expenses; 'Current liabilities' include creditors, bills payable, outstanding expenses, bank overdraft.

**Marshalling** — arranging assets and liabilities in a **particular order**:

1. **Order of liquidity** — assets in order of how easily they convert into cash (most liquid first: cash, bank, … land last); liabilities in order of urgency of payment (current liabilities first, capital last). Common for sole proprietors and partnerships.
2. **Order of permanence** — the reverse: assets starting with the most permanent (goodwill, land, building, machinery … cash last); liabilities starting with capital, long-term loans, then current liabilities. Used by companies (Schedule III follows a vertical form, broadly permanence).

**Format (order of permanence, horizontal):**

| Liabilities | ₹ | Assets | ₹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Capital (opening) + Net profit − Drawings | | Non-current assets: Goodwill, Land, Building, Plant & machinery, Furniture, Vehicles | |
| Long-term loans | | Investments (long-term) | |
| Current liabilities: Creditors, Bills payable, Outstanding expenses, Bank overdraft | | Current assets: Closing stock, Debtors, Bills receivable, Prepaid expenses, Bank, Cash | |
| **Total** | | **Total** | |

**Classification recap:** **Current assets** are expected to be realised within 12 months or the operating cycle; **non-current assets** are held for long-term use (tangible: land, building; intangible: goodwill, patents). **Current liabilities** are payable within 12 months; **non-current liabilities** (long-term borrowings) after 12 months. **Capital** is owner's equity.

sections.h: From trial balance to statements: the full example
sections.md:
**Anita Stationers — Trial Balance as at 31 March 2026 (₹):**

Debits: Opening stock 30,000; Purchases 2,40,000; Returns inward 10,000; Wages 20,000; Carriage inwards 6,000; Freight 4,000; Salaries 48,000; Rent 24,000; Advertisement 12,000; Discount allowed 3,000; Drawings 16,000; Debtors 70,000; Cash 15,000; Bank 45,000; Furniture 50,000; Machinery 1,20,000. **Total 7,13,000.**

rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch01-living-worl.title: The Living World
rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch01-living-worl.subtitle: Nearly two million named species and counting — how biologists name, sort and keep track of life

sections.h: A mango by any other name

sections.md:
We instinctively know a dog is alive and a stone is not. But defining 'living' is surprisingly hard. Biologists look for a set of characteristics.

**1. Growth.** Living organisms increase in **mass and number of cells**. Plants grow throughout life by cell division in specific regions (meristems); animals grow up to a certain age, though cell division continues to replace lost cells. In unicellular organisms, growth and reproduction are linked (division increases number). **But** growth is not a defining property: non-living things like mountains, sand mounds and crystals also 'grow' by **accumulation of material on the surface (extrinsic growth)**, whereas living growth is from **inside (intrinsic)**. Dead organisms do not grow.

**2. Reproduction.** Producing progeny similar to parents. Sexual reproduction in multicellular organisms; asexual methods too — **budding in yeast and Hydra**, **fragmentation** in filamentous algae, fungi and the protonema of mosses, **true regeneration** in Planaria (flatworms), spores in fungi. In unicellular organisms (bacteria, Amoeba, unicellular algae) reproduction = growth by cell division. **But** reproduction is not all-inclusive: **mules, sterile worker bees and infertile human couples** do not reproduce and yet are alive. So it too cannot be a defining feature.

**3. Metabolism.** The sum total of all **chemical reactions** occurring in the body — constantly making and breaking molecules. All living organisms (unicellular and multicellular) show metabolism. **No non-living object shows metabolism.** Metabolic reactions can be demonstrated **outside** the body in a test tube (*in vitro*), but these isolated reactions are not living. So metabolism is a **defining feature** of living organisms.

**4. Cellular organisation.** All living things are made of one or more cells; organisation of the body is the defining feature of life forms.

**5. Consciousness — response to stimuli.** All organisms sense their environment and respond to physical, chemical or biological stimuli — light, water, temperature, other organisms, pollutants. Plants respond to light (photoperiod affects flowering); prokaryotes to their surroundings. **Humans** are the only organisms aware of themselves — **self-consciousness**. Consciousness is therefore a **defining property** of living organisms.

**The puzzle:** a patient in an irreversible coma, supported by machines, shows no consciousness or self-awareness — is he living or dead? This is where biology meets ethics and law.

NCERT's conclusion: living organisms are **self-replicating, evolving and self-regulating interactive systems capable of responding to external stimuli**. Biology is the story of life on earth — and of evolution of living organisms.

sections.md:
Look around — the neem tree, the house sparrow, the mould on old bread, the bacteria in curd, the earthworm after the monsoon rain. Each place has its own set of organisms. The number and types of organisms on earth is called **biodiversity**.

- The number of **known and described species** is between **1.7 and 1.8 million** (NCERT's figure). Many more remain undiscovered — estimates of the total run to several million.
- New species are found every year, especially in forests, oceans and among insects and microbes. India alone, a **mega-diverse** country, has about 7–8% of recorded species on only 2.4% of the world's land.

With so many organisms, we need **standardised names** and a **system of grouping**. Local names vary from place to place, even within a country, and lead to confusion. Hence two linked processes: **nomenclature** (naming) and **classification** (grouping). Before an organism can be named, it must be correctly described — **identification**.

**Did you know?** The Western Ghats and the Eastern Himalaya are two of India's biodiversity hotspots; new frog and lizard species are still being described there regularly.

check.q: According to NCERT, the number of described species is about…
check.why: Between 1.7 and 1.8 million species have been described, with many more yet to be discovered.

sections.md:
**Nomenclature** is the process of standardising names of living organisms so that a particular organism is known by the **same name all over the world**. It is possible only when the organism is described correctly and we know to what organism the name is attached — i.e. **identification** comes first.

**Codes of nomenclature:**

- For plants: **International Code of Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN)** (now called the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants, ICN).
- For animals: **International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN)**.

These codes ensure each organism has **one scientific name**, and that the name has not been used for any other known organism.

**Binomial nomenclature**, given by **Carolus Linnaeus** (Swedish botanist, 18th century, *Species Plantarum* 1753), gives each organism a two-part name:

1. **Generic name** (genus) — first word.
2. **Specific epithet** (species) — second word.

Example: ***Mangifera indica*** — *Mangifera* is the genus, *indica* the specific epithet. Others: ***Homo sapiens*** (human), ***Panthera leo*** (lion), ***Panthera tigris*** (tiger), ***Solanum tuberosum*** (potato), ***Solanum nigrum***, ***Solanum melongena*** (brinjal), ***Musca domestica*** (housefly), ***Triticum aestivum*** (wheat), ***Felis catus*** (cat).

**Universal rules of nomenclature:**

1. Biological names are generally in **Latin** (or Latinised) and written in **italics** — they are Latinised or derived from Latin irrespective of their origin.
2. The **first word** is the genus; the **second** is the specific epithet.
3. When **handwritten**, both words are **separately underlined**; when printed, they are in **italics** — to show their Latin origin.
4. The genus starts with a **capital letter**; the specific epithet with a **small letter**.
5. The **name of the author** who first described the species appears after the specific epithet, in abbreviated form, in roman type: ***Mangifera indica* Linn.** — 'Linn.' indicates Linnaeus described it first.

So the mango's name is written: *Mangifera indica* Linn. (or Mangifera indica, each word underlined, by hand).
keyTerms: Nomenclature — standardised naming
Binomial — two-word scientific name
ICBN / ICZN — codes for plant and animal names
Specific epithet — second word of a binomial

check.q: Which is the correct way to write the scientific name of the tiger in print?
check.why: Genus starts with a capital, species with a small letter, and both are italicised in print.

sections.md:
**Classification** is the process by which anything is grouped into **convenient categories based on some easily observable characters**. We do this daily: we say 'plants' or 'animals', 'mammals', 'dogs', 'cats', 'wheat', 'rice'. Each such group is a **taxon** (plural **taxa**). Taxa can be at different levels: 'plants' is a taxon, 'wheat' is a taxon, 'animals', 'mammals', 'dogs' are taxa.

Human beings have always classified organisms, initially for **use** — food, shelter, clothing. Hence early classifications were based on **uses**.

**Taxonomy** is the branch that includes **characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification**. The processes:

- **Characterisation** — describing the features of an organism.
- **Identification** — determining the correct place of an organism among known groups.
- **Nomenclature** — giving the correct name.
- **Classification** — placing it in a group.

Modern taxonomic studies use **external and internal structure, cell structure, development process and ecological information**.

**Systematics** — the word comes from Latin *systema*, meaning **systematic arrangement** of organisms. Linnaeus used *Systema Naturae* as the title of his book. Systematics takes into account **evolutionary relationships** between organisms, in addition to identification, nomenclature and classification. It is the study of the **diversity of organisms and all their comparative and evolutionary relationships**.

| Term | Covers |
|---|---|
| Taxonomy | Characterisation, identification, nomenclature, classification |
| Systematics | All the above + evolutionary relationships |

check.q: How does systematics differ from taxonomy?
check.why: Systematics includes taxonomy but adds the study of evolutionary relationships among organisms.

sections.md:
Classification is not a single step; it involves a **hierarchy of steps** in which each step represents a **rank or category**. Since the category is part of an overall arrangement, it is called a **taxonomic category**, and all categories together form the **taxonomic hierarchy**. Each category, referred to as a unit of classification, represents a rank and is commonly termed a **taxon**.

The **obligate categories**, from lowest to highest:

**Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum (animals) / Division (plants) → Kingdom**

**Species.** A group of individual organisms with **fundamental similarities**. We can distinguish one species from closely related species based on distinct morphological differences. In *Mangifera indica*, *Solanum tuberosum* and *Panthera leo*, the words *indica*, *tuberosum* and *leo* are specific epithets. *Panthera* has another species, *tigris*; *Solanum* has *nigrum* and *melongena*. Human beings belong to the species *sapiens* of genus *Homo*.

**Genus.** A group of **related species** with more characters in common compared to species of other genera. Potato, tomato and brinjal are three species all in genus *Solanum*. Lion (*Panthera leo*), leopard (*P. pardus*) and tiger (*P. tigris*) are species of genus *Panthera*. *Panthera* differs from *Felis* (cats).

**Family.** A group of **related genera** with still fewer similarities than genus and species. Families are characterised on vegetative and reproductive features of plants. *Solanum*, *Petunia* and *Datura* are in family **Solanaceae**. Among animals, *Panthera* and *Felis* are in family **Felidae**; cat and dog are in different families — **Felidae** and **Canidae**.

**Order.** A higher category — an assemblage of families with a few similar characters. Plant families **Convolvulaceae** and **Solanaceae** are in order **Polemoniales**, mainly based on floral characters. Animal order **Carnivora** includes families Felidae and Canidae.

**Class.** Includes related orders. Order **Primata** (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) and order **Carnivora** (tiger, cat, dog) are in class **Mammalia**, which also has other orders.

**Phylum / Division.** Classes with a few common features form a phylum (animals) or division (plants). Fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals form phylum **Chordata**, based on common features like a **notochord** and **dorsal hollow neural system**. In plants, classes with few similar characters are assigned to a **division**.

**Kingdom.** The highest category. All animals belong to **Kingdom Animalia**; plants to **Kingdom Plantae**. (In Chapter 2 you will meet the five kingdoms.)

As we go **up** the hierarchy from species to kingdom, the **number of common characteristics decreases** and the number of organisms included **increases**. The lower the taxon, the more characteristics members share; the higher the category, the greater the difficulty of determining relationships to other taxa at the same level.

Taxonomists also use **sub-categories** (sub-species, sub-family, super-class, etc.) to place organisms more precisely.

sections.md:
NCERT gives a table of organisms with their categories — learn to read it, not just memorise it:

| Common name | Biological name | Genus | Family | Order | Class | Phylum/Division |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Man | *Homo sapiens* | *Homo* | Hominidae | Primata | Mammalia | Chordata |
| Housefly | *Musca domestica* | *Musca* | Muscidae | Diptera | Insecta | Arthropoda |
| Mango | *Mangifera indica* | *Mangifera* | Anacardiaceae | Sapindales | Dicotyledonae | Angiospermae |
| Wheat | *Triticum aestivum* | *Triticum* | Poaceae | Poales | Monocotyledonae | Angiospermae |

Notice: man and housefly share only Kingdom Animalia; mango and wheat share Division Angiospermae (flowering plants) but are in different classes (dicots and monocots).

**Practice the logic:** Potato (*Solanum tuberosum*) and brinjal (*Solanum melongena*) share genus, family Solanaceae, order Polemoniales, class Dicotyledonae and division Angiospermae — so they are very closely related. Potato and wheat are related only up to division.

check.q: Mango and wheat belong to the same…
check.why: Both are flowering plants, but mango is a dicot and wheat a monocot, so they first meet at the division level.

sections.md:
Taxonomic studies need correct identification — which requires **field studies, laboratory work and collections**. These collections and tools are called **taxonomical aids**.

**1. Herbarium.** A store-house of collected plant specimens that are **dried, pressed and preserved on sheets**. Sheets are arranged according to a universally accepted system of classification. Each sheet carries a **label** with the date and place of collection, English, local and botanical names, family, collector's name. Herbaria serve as **quick referral systems**. The Central National Herbarium in Howrah (Kolkata) is among India's largest.

**2. Botanical gardens.** Have collections of **living plants** for reference. Plant species are grown for identification, and each plant is **labelled** with its botanical/scientific name and family. Famous ones: **Royal Botanical Gardens, Kew (England)**; **Indian Botanical Garden, Howrah** (Acharya Jagadish Chandra Bose Indian Botanic Garden); **National Botanical Research Institute, Lucknow**.

**3. Museums.** Have collections of preserved plant and animal specimens for study and reference. Specimens are preserved in containers or jars in **preservative solutions** (formalin). Plant and animal specimens may also be preserved as dry specimens. **Insects** are preserved in insect boxes after collecting, killing and pinning. Larger animals like birds and mammals are usually **stuffed** and preserved. Museums often have collections of **skeletons** too. Schools and colleges have museums too.

**4. Zoological parks (zoos).** Places where **wild animals are kept in protected environments** under human care, enabling us to learn about their food habits and behaviour. Animals are provided, as far as possible, conditions similar to their natural habitats. Children love visiting them — e.g. Nehru Zoological Park, Hyderabad; Arignar Anna Zoological Park, Chennai.

**5. Keys.** Taxonomic **keys** help identify plants and animals based on similarities and dissimilarities. Keys are based on **contrasting characters in pairs, called couplets**. Each statement in a key is called a **lead**. Separate keys are needed for each taxonomic category — family, genus, species. Keys are generally **analytical** in nature.

**6. Flora, manuals, monographs and catalogues.** These record descriptions:

- **Flora** — the actual account of the habitat and distribution of plants of a given area; provides an index to the plant species found there.
- **Manuals** — useful in providing information for identification of names of species found in an area.
- **Monographs** — information on any **one taxon**.
- **Catalogues** — alphabetical lists of species with descriptions.

parts.md: Priya, a first-year BSc student in Kolkata, is volunteering at the Central National Herbarium. Her supervisor hands her a yellowed sheet: a dried fern, a faded label in copperplate writing — 'Darjeeling, 1890'. Her task: check whether the name on the label is still valid. She opens the flora, then a modern key. Leaf margins entire or toothed? Toothed. Spores in lines or round clusters? Round. Step by step, couplet by couplet, she reaches a species — but its name has changed since 1890, because botanists later moved it to a different genus.

Priya writes a new determination slip: the current binomial, the author's abbreviation, the date and her initials. She realises the sheet is a time machine — it proves this fern grew in Darjeeling 135 years ago. If it has vanished from there today, this sheet is evidence of change. Nomenclature, identification, classification and taxonomical aids — the whole chapter — had come together on one sheet of paper. 'Taxonomy is not just naming,' her supervisor smiles. 'It is the memory of life on earth.'

rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch02-biological-.title: Biological Classification
rd-school-c11-biology-a.ch02-biological-.subtitle: From Aristotle's two groups to Whittaker's five kingdoms — and the strange things (viruses, prions) that fit nowhere

sections.md:
Since the dawn of civilisation, humans have tried to classify living organisms — initially on the basis of their **uses** (food, shelter, clothing). **Aristotle** was the earliest to attempt a more scientific basis: he classified **plants** by simple morphological characters into **trees, shrubs and herbs**, and **animals** into two groups — those **with red blood** and those **without**.

**Linnaeus** later proposed a **Two Kingdom system**: **Plantae** and **Animalia**, containing all plants and animals respectively. It was used till very recently, but it had serious problems: it **did not distinguish** between **eukaryotes and prokaryotes**, **unicellular and multicellular** organisms, and **photosynthetic (green algae) and non-photosynthetic (fungi)** organisms. Bacteria, blue-green algae, fungi, mosses, ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms were all lumped under 'plants' simply because they had a cell wall — though they differ hugely. Characters like cell wall made fungi 'plants', and Euglena (with chlorophyll but no cell wall) confused everyone.

So a new system was needed that considered not only morphology but also **cell structure, nature of wall, mode of nutrition, habitat, methods of reproduction and evolutionary relationships**. The criteria for classification have changed over time.

**R.H. Whittaker (1969)** proposed a **Five Kingdom Classification**: **Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia**. The main criteria he used:

1. **Cell structure** (prokaryotic / eukaryotic)
2. **Body organisation** (unicellular / multicellular; tissue level)
3. **Mode of nutrition** (autotrophic / heterotrophic — saprophytic, parasitic, holozoic)
4. **Reproduction**
5. **Phylogenetic (evolutionary) relationships**

Under this system, unicellular organisms were brought into Monera (prokaryotes) and Protista (eukaryotes); fungi were separated from plants. (Later, Carl Woese proposed a **three-domain** system — Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya — and a six-kingdom system, but NCERT uses Whittaker's.)

options: Did not distinguish prokaryotes from eukaryotes, or fungi from green plants
check.why: Grouping by cell wall put bacteria, fungi and green plants together despite fundamental differences.

sections.md:
**Bacteria** are the sole members of Kingdom Monera. They are the **most abundant** micro-organisms, occurring almost everywhere — hundreds of them in a handful of soil; in **extreme habitats** like hot springs, deserts, snow and deep oceans where very few other life forms survive; and many live as **parasites** in or on other organisms.

**Shapes** (four basic):

- **Coccus** (spherical, plural cocci)
- **Bacillus** (rod-shaped)
- **Vibrium** (comma-shaped)
- **Spirillum** (spiral)

Though structurally simple, bacteria are **very complex in behaviour** and show the most extensive **metabolic diversity**. Some are **autotrophic** — they synthesise their own food from inorganic substrates; they may be **photosynthetic** or **chemosynthetic**. Most are **heterotrophs** — they depend on other organisms or on dead organic matter.

**1. Archaebacteria.** Special bacteria living in the **harshest habitats**: **extreme salty areas (halophiles)**, **hot springs (thermoacidophiles)** and **marshy areas (methanogens)**. They differ from other bacteria in having a **different cell wall structure**, which is responsible for their survival in extreme conditions. **Methanogens** are present in the **gut of ruminant animals** (cows, buffaloes) and are responsible for the production of **methane (biogas)** from their dung — the basis of gobar gas plants in Indian villages.

**2. Eubacteria ('true bacteria').** Characterised by a **rigid cell wall** and, if motile, a **flagellum**.

- **Cyanobacteria** (blue-green algae) have **chlorophyll a** similar to green plants and are **photosynthetic autotrophs**. They are unicellular, colonial or filamentous, freshwater/marine or terrestrial. Colonies are generally surrounded by a gelatinous sheath. They often form **blooms** in polluted water bodies. Some, like ***Nostoc*** and ***Anabaena***, can **fix atmospheric nitrogen** in specialised cells called **heterocysts** — important for rice paddies.
- **Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria** oxidise various inorganic substances such as **nitrates, nitrites and ammonia** and use the released energy for ATP production. They play a great role in **recycling nutrients** like nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and sulphur.
- **Heterotrophic bacteria** are the most abundant in nature. The majority are important **decomposers**. Many have significant impact on human affairs: making **curd from milk** (*Lactobacillus*), production of **antibiotics**, **fixing nitrogen in legume roots** (*Rhizobium*). Some are **pathogens** causing damage to humans, crops, farm animals and pets: **cholera, typhoid, tetanus, citrus canker** are well-known bacterial diseases.

**Reproduction.** Bacteria reproduce mainly by **fission**. Sometimes, under unfavourable conditions, they produce **spores**. They also reproduce by a sort of **sexual reproduction** by adopting a primitive type of **DNA transfer** from one bacterium to another.

**Mycoplasma** are organisms that **completely lack a cell wall**. They are the **smallest living cells known** and can survive **without oxygen**. Many are pathogenic in animals and plants.

sections.md:
All **single-celled eukaryotes** are placed under **Protista**, but the boundaries of this kingdom are not well defined — what one biologist calls a 'photosynthetic protistan' another may call a plant. Members are **primarily aquatic**. Protista forms a **link** with the others dealing with plants, animals and fungi. Being eukaryotes, the protistan cell has a **well-defined nucleus** and other membrane-bound organelles. Some have **flagella or cilia**. They reproduce **asexually and sexually** by a process involving **cell fusion and zygote formation**.

**1. Chrysophytes** — **diatoms** and **golden algae (desmids)**. Found in **fresh water and marine** environments. **Microscopic** and float passively in water currents (**plankton**). Most are **photosynthetic**. In diatoms, the cell walls form **two thin overlapping shells**, which fit together as in a **soap box**. The walls are embedded with **silica** and thus are **indestructible**. So diatoms have left behind large amounts of cell wall deposits in their habitat; this accumulation over billions of years is called **'diatomaceous earth'**. Being gritty, this soil is used in **polishing, filtration of oils and syrups**. Diatoms are the **chief 'producers' in the oceans**.

**2. Dinoflagellates** — mostly **marine and photosynthetic**. They appear **yellow, green, brown, blue or red** depending on the main pigments in their cells. The cell wall has **stiff cellulose plates** on the outer surface. Most have **two flagella**: one lies **longitudinally** and the other **transversely** in a furrow between the wall plates. Very often **red dinoflagellates** (e.g. ***Gonyaulax***) undergo such rapid multiplication that they make the sea appear red (**red tides**). Toxins released by such large numbers may even **kill other marine animals such as fishes**.

**3. Euglenoids** — majority are **freshwater** organisms found in stagnant water. Instead of a cell wall, they have a **protein-rich layer called pellicle**, which makes their body **flexible**. They have **two flagella, a short and a long one**. Though **photosynthetic in the presence of sunlight**, when deprived of sunlight they behave like **heterotrophs** by predating on other smaller organisms. Interestingly, the pigments of euglenoids are **identical to those of higher plants**. Example: ***Euglena***.

**4. Slime moulds** — **saprophytic** protists. The body moves along **decaying twigs and leaves**, engulfing organic material. Under suitable conditions, they form an aggregation called **plasmodium**, which may grow and spread over **several feet**. During unfavourable conditions, the plasmodium differentiates and forms **fruiting bodies** bearing **spores** at their tips. The spores possess **true walls**; they are **extremely resistant** and survive for many years, even under adverse conditions. The spores are **dispersed by air currents**.

**5. Protozoans** — all **heterotrophs**, living as **predators or parasites**. They are believed to be **primitive relatives of animals**. Four major groups:

- **Amoeboid protozoans** — live in fresh water, sea water or moist soil. They move and capture prey by putting out **pseudopodia (false feet)**, as in ***Amoeba***. Marine forms have **silica shells** on their surface. Some, such as ***Entamoeba***, are **parasites** (amoebic dysentery).
- **Flagellated protozoans** — free-living or parasitic, with **flagella**. Parasitic forms cause diseases such as **sleeping sickness** — e.g. ***Trypanosoma***.
- **Ciliated protozoans** — aquatic, actively moving organisms because of thousands of **cilia**. They have a **cavity (gullet)** that opens to the outside of the cell surface. Coordinated movement of rows of cilia causes the water laden with food to be steered into the gullet. Example: ***Paramoecium***.
- **Sporozoans** — diverse organisms that have an **infectious spore-like stage** in their life cycle. The most notorious is ***Plasmodium*** (malarial parasite), which causes **malaria** — a disease with a staggering effect on human population.

sections.md:
Fungi form a unique kingdom of **heterotrophic** organisms showing great diversity in morphology and habitat. You have seen fungi on **moist bread and rotten fruits**. The common **mushroom** and **toadstools** are fungi. White spots on mustard leaves are due to a **parasitic fungus**. Some unicellular fungi, **yeast**, are used to make **bread and beer**. Others cause diseases in plants and animals: **wheat rust** is caused by ***Puccinia***. Some are the source of **antibiotics**, e.g. ***Penicillium***. Fungi are **cosmopolitan**, occurring in air, water, soil and on animals and plants; they prefer **warm and humid** places — which is why we keep food in the refrigerator.

**Structure.** With the exception of yeasts (unicellular), fungi are **filamentous**. Their bodies consist of long, slender thread-like structures called **hyphae**. The network of hyphae is called **mycelium**. Some hyphae are continuous tubes filled with **multinucleated cytoplasm** — **coenocytic hyphae**. Others have **septae** or cross walls. The **cell walls are composed of chitin and polysaccharides**.

**Nutrition.** Most fungi are **heterotrophic** and absorb soluble organic matter from **dead substrates** — **saprophytes**. Those depending on living plants and animals are **parasites**. They can also live as **symbionts** — in association with algae as **lichens** and with roots of higher plants as **mycorrhiza**.

**Reproduction.**

- **Vegetative:** fragmentation, fission and budding.
- **Asexual:** by spores called **conidia** or **sporangiospores** or **zoospores**.
- **Sexual:** by **oospores, ascospores and basidiospores**, produced in distinct structures called **fruiting bodies**.

The sexual cycle involves three steps: (i) **Plasmogamy** — fusion of protoplasms between two motile or non-motile gametes; (ii) **Karyogamy** — fusion of two nuclei; (iii) **Meiosis** in the zygote resulting in haploid spores. In some fungi (ascomycetes and basidiomycetes), when two haploid hyphae of compatible mating types fuse, an intervening **dikaryotic stage (n + n, two nuclei per cell)** occurs — the **dikaryophase**; later the parental nuclei fuse and the cells become diploid. Fruiting bodies are formed where reduction division occurs, giving haploid spores.

**Classes** (based on morphology of mycelium, mode of spore formation and fruiting bodies):

| Class | Mycelium | Asexual spores | Sexual spores | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Phycomycetes** | Aseptate, coenocytic; in aquatic habitats, decaying wood, or obligate parasites on plants | Zoospores (motile) or aplanospores (non-motile), endogenous in sporangium | **Zygospore** (fusion of two gametes, isogamous or anisogamous/oogamous) | ***Mucor*, *Rhizopus*** (bread mould), ***Albugo*** (parasitic on mustard) |
| **Ascomycetes** ('sac-fungi') | Mostly multicellular; septate and branched; some unicellular (yeast) | **Conidia** — produced exogenously on special mycelium called **conidiophores**; germinate to form mycelium | **Ascospores**, produced endogenously in sac-like **asci**, arranged in fruiting bodies called **ascocarps** | ***Aspergillus*, *Claviceps*, *Neurospora*** (used in biochemical and genetic work), *Saccharomyces* (yeast); morels and truffles are edible delicacies. Saprophytic, decomposers, parasitic or coprophilous (on dung) |
| **Basidiomycetes** | Septate, branched | Generally absent; vegetative reproduction by fragmentation is common | Sex organs absent; plasmogamy by fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains; resulting structure is dikaryotic which ultimately gives rise to **basidium**; karyogamy and meiosis in the basidium produce four **basidiospores** exogenously; basidia arranged in **basidiocarps** | **Mushrooms (*Agaricus*), bracket fungi, puffballs**; ***Ustilago*** (smut), ***Puccinia*** (rust) |
| **Deuteromycetes** ('imperfect fungi') | Septate, branched | Asexual spores — **conidia** only | **Sexual phase not known**; when the sexual form is discovered they are moved to ascomycetes or basidiomycetes | ***Alternaria*, *Colletotrichum*, *Trichoderma***. Some are saprophytes or parasites; a large number are **decomposers of litter** and help in mineral cycling |

check.q: A fungus with septate hyphae that produces ascospores in asci belongs to…
check.why: Ascomycetes ('sac fungi') bear sexual ascospores inside sac-like asci in ascocarps.

sections.md:
**Kingdom Plantae** includes all **eukaryotic, chlorophyll-containing organisms** commonly called plants. A few members are **partially heterotrophic** — the **insectivorous plants** such as **bladderwort** and **Venus flytrap**, or **parasites** like ***Cuscuta*** (dodder, the yellow vine seen on hedges). Plant cells have a eukaryotic structure with prominent **chloroplasts** and a cell wall mainly made of **cellulose**.

Plantae includes **algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms** (studied in Chapter 3, Plant Kingdom). Life cycle of plants has two distinct phases — the **diploid sporophytic** and the **haploid gametophytic** — that alternate with each other. The lengths of the haploid and diploid phases, and whether these phases are free-living or dependent on others, vary among groups. This phenomenon is called **alternation of generations**.

**Kingdom Animalia** is characterised by **heterotrophic eukaryotic organisms** that are **multicellular** and whose cells **lack cell walls**. They directly or indirectly depend on plants for food. They digest their food in an **internal cavity** and store food reserves as **glycogen or fat**. Their mode of nutrition is **holozoic** — by ingestion of food. They follow a **definite growth pattern** and grow into adults that have a definite shape and size. Higher forms show elaborate **sensory and neuromotor mechanisms**. Most are capable of **locomotion**. **Sexual reproduction** is by **copulation of male and female** followed by **embryological development**. (Details in Chapter 4, Animal Kingdom.)

left.title: Plantae
points: Few partial heterotrophs: Venus flytrap, bladderwort, Cuscuta

right.title: Animalia
points: Food stored as glycogen or fat
Definite growth pattern; most move; copulation and embryo development

check.q: Cuscuta is placed in Plantae although it is…
options: A parasite that is partially heterotrophic
check.why: Cuscuta is a flowering plant that lives as a parasite, so it is a partially heterotrophic member of Plantae.

sections.md:
Whittaker's five kingdoms leave out some **acellular** organisms like **viruses and viroids**, and **lichens**.

**Viruses.** We have all suffered the ill effects of common cold or 'flu'. Viruses **did not find a place** in classification because they are not considered truly 'living', if we understand living as organisms that have a cell structure. Viruses are **non-cellular** organisms characterised by an **inert crystalline structure outside the living cell**. Once they infect a cell, they **take over the machinery** of the host cell to replicate themselves, killing the host. So: are they living or non-living?

- The name **virus**, meaning **venom or poisonous fluid**, was given by **Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892)**, who recognised certain microbes as the causal organism of **mosaic disease of tobacco**. These were found to be **smaller than bacteria** because they passed through **bacteria-proof filters**.
- **M.W. Beijerinck (1898)** demonstrated that the extract of infected tobacco plants could cause infection in healthy plants and called the fluid ***Contagium vivum fluidum*** (infectious living fluid).
- **W.M. Stanley (1935)** showed that viruses could be **crystallised**, and the crystals consist largely of **proteins**. They are **inert outside** their specific host cell. Viruses are **obligate parasites**.

**Structure.** In addition to proteins, viruses contain **genetic material** that could be **either RNA or DNA** — **no virus contains both**. A virus is a **nucleoprotein** and the genetic material is **infectious**. In general, viruses that infect **plants have single-stranded RNA**, and viruses that infect **animals have single- or double-stranded RNA or double-stranded DNA**. **Bacterial viruses or bacteriophages** (viruses that infect bacteria) are usually **double-stranded DNA** viruses. The protein coat, called **capsid**, made of small subunits called **capsomeres**, protects the nucleic acid. These capsomeres are arranged in **helical or polyhedral** geometric forms.

**Diseases.** Viruses cause **mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza** and **AIDS** in humans (and COVID-19, caused by a coronavirus). In plants, symptoms include **mosaic formation, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing and vein clearing, dwarfing and stunted growth**.

**Viroids.** In **1971**, **T.O. Diener** discovered a new infectious agent smaller than viruses that caused **potato spindle tuber disease**. It was found to be a **free RNA**; it **lacked the protein coat** found in viruses, hence the name **viroid**. The RNA of the viroid was of **low molecular weight**.

**Prions.** In modern medicine certain infectious **neurological diseases** were found to be transmitted by an agent consisting of **abnormally folded protein**. The agent was similar in size to viruses. These agents are called **prions**. The most notable diseases caused by prions are **bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE)**, commonly called **mad cow disease** in cattle, and its analogous variant **Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD)** in humans.

**Lichens.** **Symbiotic associations** — mutually useful associations — between **algae and fungi**. The algal component is the **phycobiont** and the fungal component the **mycobiont**; they are **autotrophic and heterotrophic** respectively. Algae prepare food for fungi, and fungi provide **shelter** and **absorb mineral nutrients and water** for their partner. So close is their association that if one saw a lichen in nature one would never imagine they had two different organisms within them. Lichens are very good **pollution indicators** — they **do not grow in polluted areas**.

check.q: Viroids differ from viruses in that viroids…
options: Lack a protein coat and are free RNA
check.why: Diener's viroid is a small free RNA without the protein capsid that viruses have.

story.title: A Curd, a Cow and a Cold

parts.md: Sunday morning in Pune. Aarav's mother sets milk to curdle with a spoon of yesterday's curd — **Lactobacillus**, a heterotrophic eubacterium, gets to work (Monera). At the dairy farm his uncle runs, the cows' dung goes into a biogas plant where **methanogens** — archaebacteria from the cows' own gut — turn it into cooking gas. The pond behind the farm has turned green with a **cyanobacterial bloom**, a sign of too much fertiliser running in. On the bread in the kitchen, a fuzzy black patch: ***Rhizopus***, a phycomycete fungus.

By afternoon Aarav has a runny nose — a **virus**, which is neither in Monera nor in any kingdom at all. At the doctor's clinic a poster warns about malaria (***Plasmodium***, a sporozoan protist) during the monsoon. On the walk home he notices grey-green crusts on an old temple wall — **lichens**, a fungus and an alga living as one, and a sign the air there is still clean. 'Five kingdoms before dinner,' he laughs, 'and two things that refuse to join any of them.'

summary: Aristotle grouped plants as trees, shrubs, herbs and animals by red blood; Linnaeus proposed two kingdoms.
The two-kingdom system failed to separate prokaryotes/eukaryotes, unicellular/multicellular, photosynthetic/non-photosynthetic organisms.
Whittaker (1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia — based on cell structure, body organisation, nutrition, reproduction, phylogeny.
Monera = bacteria; shapes coccus, bacillus, vibrio, spirillum; huge metabolic diversity.
Archaebacteria (halophiles, thermoacidophiles, methanogens) have a different cell wall; methanogens make biogas.
Eubacteria: cyanobacteria (chlorophyll a, heterocysts in Nostoc, Anabaena), chemosynthetic and heterotrophic bacteria.
Bacteria reproduce by fission, spores, and primitive DNA transfer; mycoplasma lack walls and are the smallest cells.
Protista: single-celled eukaryotes — chrysophytes (diatoms), dinoflagellates (red tides), euglenoids (pellicle), slime moulds (plasmodium), protozoans (amoeboid, flagellated, ciliated, sporozoans).
Fungi: heterotrophic, hyphae and mycelium, chitin walls; plasmogamy, karyogamy, meiosis; dikaryophase.
Fungal classes: Phycomycetes (zygospores), Ascomycetes (ascospores), Basidiomycetes (basidiospores), Deuteromycetes (no known sexual stage).
Plantae: eukaryotic, chlorophyll, cellulose walls, alternation of generations; Animalia: heterotrophic, no cell walls, holozoic.
Viruses: non-cellular nucleoproteins with DNA or RNA, obligate parasites (Ivanowsky, Beijerinck, Stanley).
Viroids are free RNA (Diener 1971); prions are misfolded proteins (BSE, CJD).
Lichens are algae–fungus symbioses and pollution indicators.

sections.h: A walk up a hill in Shillong
sections.md:
Start beside a pond, where slimy green threads drift on the surface. These are **algae**. A little higher, a damp stone wall is covered in a soft green carpet of **mosses**. In the shade of the trees grow **ferns**, their young fronds still curled like a violin's scroll. Further up stand tall **pines** with needle leaves and woody cones. All around, from the grass under your feet to the orchids hanging on tree trunks, are the **flowering plants**.

In one hour's walk you have covered the whole chapter: **algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms**. The order also roughly follows the evolutionary story of how plants left the water and settled on land.

In Whittaker's system (previous chapter), kingdom Plantae no longer contains fungi or Monera, and single-celled algae like *Chlamydomonas* and *Chlorella* belong to Protista. Even so, the NCERT chapter still describes algae under plants, and this read does the same.

**How have plants been classified?**

- **Artificial systems** came first. They used a few obvious external features such as habit, colour, or the number and shape of leaves. Linnaeus grouped flowering plants mainly by the **androecium** (stamens). Because vegetative and sexual characters were given equal weight, closely related plants sometimes ended up far apart.
- **Natural systems** group plants by their natural similarities, using many characters: external form, internal anatomy, ultrastructure, embryology and plant chemistry. **Bentham and Hooker** produced such a system for flowering plants.
- **Phylogenetic systems** are based on evolutionary relationships. They assume that members of a group share a common ancestor.

Newer evidence helps sort out difficult cases. In **numerical taxonomy**, computers handle hundreds of characters at once, each given a code and equal importance. **Cytotaxonomy** uses chromosome number, structure and behaviour. **Chemotaxonomy** uses the chemicals a plant makes.

check.q: Linnaeus's artificial system of plant classification was based mainly on:
check.why: Linnaeus classified flowering plants largely by the number and arrangement of stamens (androecium), an artificial single-character approach.

sections.h: Algae: the green of the waters
sections.md:
**Algae** are simple plants that contain chlorophyll and make their own food. Their body is a **thallus**, which means it is not divided into root, stem and leaf. Most live in fresh or salt water, but they also grow on wet rocks, soil and wood. Some live in partnership with fungi as lichens, and some even grow on animals, such as in the fur of a sloth bear.

They come in every size. *Volvox* forms ball-shaped colonies, *Ulothrix* and *Spirogyra* grow as threads (filaments), and some marine **kelps** grow into huge seaweeds many metres long.

**Reproduction:**

- **Vegetative:** the thallus breaks into fragments (fragmentation), and each piece grows into a new alga.
- **Asexual:** by spores. The commonest are **zoospores**, which have flagella, swim about and then grow into new plants.
- **Sexual:** two gametes fuse. In **isogamy** the two gametes look alike and are the same size. They may both have flagella (*Chlamydomonas*) or neither may (*Spirogyra*). In **anisogamy** the gametes differ in size (some *Chlamydomonas* species). In **oogamy** a large egg that cannot move is fertilised by a small sperm that swims (*Volvox*, *Fucus*).

**Why algae matter.** Algae carry out about half of all the carbon dioxide fixation on Earth. They add oxygen to the water around them and are the base of aquatic food chains. About 70 species of seaweed are eaten, including *Porphyra*, *Laminaria* and *Sargassum*. Brown algae give **algin** and red algae give **carrageen**. These are hydrocolloids, substances that hold water, and are used in many products. **Agar**, extracted from the red algae *Gelidium* and *Gracilaria*, is used to grow microbes in laboratories and to set ice-creams and jellies. *Chlorella* is a single-celled alga rich in protein and has been used as a food supplement, even on space missions.

Algae are divided into three main classes by their pigments, stored food and other features: **Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae**.

sections.h: The three classes of algae in detail
sections.md:
**Chlorophyceae (green algae).** These may be single cells, colonies or filaments. Chlorophylls *a* and *b* give them a bright grass-green colour. The pigments are held in **chloroplasts**, whose shape varies from species to species: disc, plate, net, cup, spiral or ribbon. Most have **pyrenoids** inside the chloroplast, which store protein as well as starch, and a few store oil droplets. The cell wall has an inner cellulose layer and an outer layer of pectose. They reproduce by fragmentation, by flagellated zoospores formed in zoosporangia, and sexually by isogamy, anisogamy or oogamy. Examples: *Chlamydomonas*, *Volvox*, *Ulothrix*, *Spirogyra*, *Chara*.

**Phaeophyceae (brown algae).** Almost all are marine. They range from small branched filaments such as *Ectocarpus* to giant **kelps** up to about 100 m long. Besides chlorophylls *a* and *c*, they contain carotenoids and xanthophylls. The amount of the brown pigment **fucoxanthin** decides whether they look olive-green or dark brown. They store food as **laminarin** or **mannitol**. The cellulose wall has an outer jelly-like coat of **algin**. A typical large brown alga has three parts: a **holdfast** that grips the rock, a stalk called the **stipe**, and a flat, leaf-like **frond** that photosynthesises. Asexual reproduction is by pear-shaped zoospores with two unequal flagella attached at the side. Sexual reproduction may be isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous. Examples: *Ectocarpus*, *Dictyota*, *Laminaria*, *Sargassum*, *Fucus*.

**Rhodophyceae (red algae).** Their red colour comes from **r-phycoerythrin**. Most are marine and are commonest in warm seas. They grow both near the bright surface and at great depths, because phycoerythrin absorbs the blue-green light that reaches deep water. Most have many-celled thalli, some with complex organisation. Food is stored as **floridean starch**, which is similar in structure to amylopectin and glycogen. They reproduce by fragmentation, by non-motile spores, and sexually by non-motile gametes. Sexual reproduction is oogamous and is followed by complicated changes after fertilisation. Examples: *Polysiphonia*, *Porphyra*, *Gracilaria*, *Gelidium*.

> Did you know? Giant kelp can grow by up to about half a metre a day, which makes it one of the fastest-growing organisms on Earth.

check.q: Red algae can live at great depths because:
options: Phycoerythrin absorbs the blue-green light that penetrates deep water
check.why: Only shorter blue-green wavelengths reach deep water, and r-phycoerythrin is well suited to absorbing them.

sections.h: Bryophytes: amphibians of the plant kingdom
sections.md:
**Bryophytes** are the **liverworts** and **mosses** that grow in damp, shady spots, especially in the hills. They are called the **amphibians of the plant kingdom** because, like frogs, they live on land but need water to breed.

Their body is more complex than an alga's. It may lie flat or stand upright and is fixed to the ground by **rhizoids** made of one or many cells. They have no true roots, stems or leaves, though some parts look like them.

**Life cycle.** The main plant is **haploid**. Because it produces gametes, it is the **gametophyte**. Its sex organs are many-celled. The male organ, the **antheridium**, releases **antherozoids** that have two flagella. The female organ, the flask-shaped **archegonium**, holds a single egg. Antherozoids swim through a film of water to the archegonium, and one fuses with the egg to form a **zygote**. The zygote does not undergo meiosis straight away. It grows by mitosis into a many-celled **sporophyte**, which is **not free-living**. It stays attached to the green gametophyte and takes food from it. Some sporophyte cells then divide by meiosis to form haploid spores, and each spore grows into a new gametophyte.

**Importance.** Some mosses are food for grazing mammals and birds. Dried *Sphagnum* moss forms **peat**, which is burnt as fuel. Because it holds a lot of water, it is also used to pack living plants for transport. Mosses and lichens are among the **first organisms to colonise bare rock**. They slowly break the rock down and make soil in which larger plants can grow, and their dense mats soften the impact of raindrops and so reduce soil erosion.

**Liverworts** grow on stream banks, marshy ground, damp soil and tree bark. *Marchantia* has a flat thallus, with distinct upper and lower surfaces, that lies pressed against the ground. It reproduces asexually by fragmentation or by **gemmae**. These are small green buds of many cells that form in **gemma cups** on the thallus, break off and grow into new plants. Male and female sex organs may be on the same thallus or on separate ones. The sporophyte has a foot, a seta (stalk) and a capsule.

**Mosses.** The gametophyte of a moss has two stages:

1. the **protonema**, a creeping, green, branched, thread-like stage that grows straight from a spore;
2. the **leafy stage**, which grows from a side bud on the protonema. It has a slender upright axis with leaves arranged in a spiral, is held in the soil by branched rhizoids made of many cells, and carries the sex organs.

Mosses also spread vegetatively by fragmentation and by budding of the secondary protonema. The moss sporophyte is better developed than a liverwort's. Its capsule holds spores formed by meiosis and has an elaborate way of scattering them. Examples: *Funaria*, *Polytrichum*, *Sphagnum*.
